utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you very much, your Honour. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Can we have representations.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I am Eric Ostberg appearing today with Ms. Teresa McHenry, Mr. Grant Niemann and our case manager, Ms. Elles van Dusschoten. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: From the Defence? MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Good morning, your Honours. I am Edina Residovic, defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic. With me in the defence team is Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan, Professor from Canada. MR. OLUJIC (in interpretation): Good morning, your Honours. My name is Zeljko Olujic. With me is Mr. Michael Greaves. We are the Defence counsel for Mr. Zdravko Mucic. MR. KARABDIC (in interpretation): Good morning, your Honours. I am Salih Karabdic. I am defence counsel for Mr. Hazim Delic. With me in the team is Mr. Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am John Ackerman appearing on behalf of Mr. Esad Landzo. I am ably assisted today by Cynthia McMurrey. Thank you. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you very much. Can we have the witness now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps, your Honour, before that happens and arising out of the application that was made late yesterday afternoon, your Honours, first of all, if any members of the defence staff were offended by my remarks yesterday I want to extend my apologies. I hold them all in very, very high regard. I consider them colleagues of the highest professional standard. If the court was offended in any way by those remarks, I want to sincerely apologise for that also. With that, your Honours, Mr. Ostberg is now back with us and I seek your Honours' leave to withdraw for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Before my learned friend goes, I thank him for his kind apology. It is accepted in the spirit in which it was given and we thank him. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Now Mr. Grant Niemann, thank you very much for behaving in the best traditions of the Bar. We appreciate it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Can we have the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution does have a witness who is ready to appear. I don't know whether or not yesterday we had moved to have admitted into evidence certain material, including videotapes and transcripts of statements. I believe some of them may have already been admitted and maybe the Registrar could assist us, but in case there's any confusion, we do seek to have the videotapes and the transcripts of the interviews taken by the Office of the Prosecutor of Mr. Mucic, Delic and Landzo admitted into evidence. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes. I think that's what we are here for this morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Then if your Honours are waiting for Mr. Bart d'Hooge, because I believe that all that was left was legal argument rather than any additional questions, we do not have him in the witness room. He's in the building. If your Honours wish that he be present for this, we can get him. Certainly I believed, and I am sorry if I misunderstood the court, that it was legal argument. We did not think it was necessary to have him here. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Can I have any responses on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I was certainly not expecting Mr. d'Hooge to be here today and I don't think it is appropriate for him to be present during legal argument on the issues that are raised on this matter. My friend and I are ad idem on that matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: He was available outside if your Honours want him but I don't believe it's necessary. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Can we have legal arguments about the tendering of any of the documents? Let me find out from counsel. I thought from the evidence we have had here Mr. Abribat was part of the exercise of recording all questions and whether he needs to be recalled for the purposes of being examined on anything else except you are satisfied from the evidence we have had and it is not necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I certainly have no -- sorry. I will start that again. I have no application for him to be recalled and examined further by either myself or by my learned friends. I think your Honour has now heard all the evidence in relation to the OTP interviews that you can possibly hear. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: So we are satisfied that we can carry on with the arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: May it please your Honours, your Honours have, I'm sure, my motion which was filed, I think, on 8th May, and also I'm sure the Prosecution's response thereto. I don't propose to go over the ground that's set out in those documents, since that would be a pointless exercise. It's there in writing and your Honours can see the outline of the argument from that. What I would like to do this morning is to make some further submissions on matters of law and also address you on matters of fact. The defendant's case in regard to the interviews that was conducted with him in March 1996 in Vienna relate, in my submission, not just to those conducted by the Office of the Prosecution but also to the interview conducted by the Austrian police. The interviews with the Office of the Prosecution cannot be placed in some separate compartment as if it stands on its own, quite isolated from the procedures of the Austrian police. It must be seen, we respectfully submit, as simply a continuing part of an entire process that took place over a period of about four days.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you please slow down a little?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I've had a little voice whispering in my ear telling me to slow down and I shall do so. My apologies to all concerned. We submit that that process which took place over that period of time, the 18th-21st March, was flawed in such a way that the only proper conclusion that this honourable Tribunal can come to is to exclude all the interviews that were conducted with Mr. Mucic at that time. As I've indicated, I've set out, or we've set out a number of propositions of law in our motion of 8th May. So I turn now straightaway to the interview with the Austrian police. We submit this: this interview is not admissible for two principal reasons. Firstly, the manner in which the interview was procured offends against Rule 95 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. I don't propose to read that Rule out. Your Honours are well familiar with it and know exactly what it contains and what the purpose of it is. One has, in our respectful submission, to look at the document which sets out the rights of prisoners. I'm sorry. Will your Honour just give me a moment, please? That is the document which appears as Annexe 3 to the Prosecution's response to the Defence motion. Your Honour, in their response they describe the Austrian criminal procedure as having an active and caring attitude. In our respectful submission, and with considerable regret, I have to say that that is a complete fallacy. The rights afforded under Austrian law to arrested persons fall a long way short of those which this Tribunal has determined are appropriate for use in these cases. Can I remind you, first of all, please, of some of the features of that information sheet for arrested persons? Paragraph 4 of that document, in our respectful submission, offends against the spirit of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, in which it makes it quite plain that there is, quite simply, no proper right to have counsel assisting you. Can I remind you of the phraseology? It says this in the English translation: "If you want your legal counsel to come and see you as soon as possible, make it known. You may not have legal counsel present when you are questioned for a criminal offence". I pause there and respectfully remind your Honours of Rules 42 and 43 and the similar rules that exist for accused persons. Those rules make it quite plain that this Tribunal -- the view of this Tribunal is that you have a right to have counsel present during the course of interview, and you are entitled to have advice during the course of that interview. We respectfully submit that that phrase, which is read out to suspects in Austria, offends greatly against that principle. It goes on: "In that case, therefore, you will have an opportunity to see and speak to your lawyer only", and I stress the word "only", "after you have been questioned, but even then only if it has been determined that you will be transferred to the court prison and that there is sufficient time remaining until then". I stress the words "only" there, because it makes it plain, in my submission, that you do not have an unfettered right to see your counsel, and only then after the questioning has taken place. In our respectful submission, that, too, offends greatly against the rules of this Tribunal and the spirit thereof. It goes on: "Such consultation with your lawyer will, moreover, be considered only if there is no risk of prejudicing the course of justice". As you will recall from my learned friend Mr. Moran's cross-examination, it is evident that the effect of that is that you only get to see your lawyer if the police approve. To call that an active and caring attitude is, in my respectful submission, simply quite extraordinary. Any system which has a system in place which permits you only to see your lawyer if the police approve smacks, I am afraid, and I say it again, and I regret to have to say this about the Republic of Austria, smacks of the police state. It is a right which this Tribunal recognises from the word go that you have, and there is no interference with that right. Unfortunately the rights accorded to you by the Austrian criminal procedure offend against that principle. I move now to paragraph seven in the English translation of that document. This deals with the matters that have been raised about what is being said to you in order to get you to talk to the police: "You will have an opportunity to speak about the accusations against you". There is nothing wrong with that but it goes on: "If you do not use it and remain silent instead, you are depriving yourself of the possibility to give an account of things from your perspective and to defend yourself". In our respectful submission what that means is this: you have, of course, the right to remain silent, but if you don't -- if you exercise that right to remain silent, you are effectively removing your right to defend yourself. In our respectful submission, that offends against the spirit of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence that have been determined as being appropriate for this trial: "Your statements may also help to clear up a mistake. You need not speak about the case. However, in the event of a sentence, if you confess or otherwise contribute through your statements to elucidating the truth, it will be taken into account as grounds for mitigation". Of course, when you are addressing a sentencing judge, one of the features that any good counsel pleading in mitigation will advance before the learned judge is this: "Your Honour, one feature that you can take into account in sentencing this man is the fact that he, when faced with the matter, admitted it immediately to the police". That's plainly right, but if what is said in order to get the interview going is: "If you confess, it will go better for you", that, to use the phraseology that certainly two of the learned judges sitting on this Tribunal will recall from practitioners' days, the judges' rules, that amounts to an inducement. It's an inducement to confess, and one remembers only too well before the coming of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 in England how allegations were made and frequently substantiated that police officers would say to suspects who were being interviewed, for example: "You won't get bail unless you confess. We'll arrest your wife and talk to her unless you tell us what you know", and so on and so forth. The phrase: "In the event of a sentence if you confess or otherwise contribute through your statements in elucidating the truth, it will be taken into account as grounds for mitigation", that, in my respectful submission, is a clear offer, prior to interview, that: "If you confess, it will go better for you". The effect of that is this: in the mind of the listener he knows that if he confesses he'll get a lighter sentence. In the old phraseology of the common law, that is an inducement, and it offends, in our respectful submission, against the notion that the spirit of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. It goes on further: "In any case, your first statement is of considerable importance as evidence for the further proceedings". One wonders who is going to be using that evidence. Effectively it is the state that is going to use that evidence and effectively the state will want to use it against him. So everything about the way in which a defendant is approached by the Austrian police, in our respectful submission, is designed to get people to confess, whether it's true or not. Will your Honour just give me a moment, please? If I can just bring the Tribunal up-to-date with what has happened in the intervening period in my system, and I do not want to harp on about the advantages of any particular system, but it perhaps helps to see where the idea of the judges' rules has gone to. In 1984 we had a new act passed, the Police and Criminal Evidence Act, and the one which deals with confessions is Section 76. It perhaps may give some idea of how the notion has developed as to the exclusion of evidence. Section 76 of that Act says this: "In any proceedings a confession made by an accused person may be given in evidence against him in so far as it is relevant to any matter in issue in the proceedings and is not excluded by the court in pursuance of this section". Subsection 2 says this: "If in any proceedings where the Prosecution proposes to give in evidence a confession made by an accused person it is represented to the court that the confession was or may have been obtained (a) by oppression of the person who made it or (b) in consequence of anything said or done which was likely in the circumstances existing at the time to render unreliable any confession which might be made by him in consequence thereof, the court shall not allow the confession to be given in evidence against him, except in so far as the Prosecution proves to the court beyond reasonable doubt".

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If counsel could please just slow down for interpretation. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: " ... except in so far as the Prosecution proves to the court beyond reasonable doubt that the confession, notwithstanding that it may be true, was not obtained as aforesaid". The definition of confession is this: "Confession includes any statement wholly or partly adverse to the person who made it, whether made to a person in authority or not, and whether made in words or otherwise". In essence, that is a statutory codification of the rules which had become well-known throughout the Commonwealth, common law jurisdictions as the judges' rules and in essence re states those rules. I present that codification in this way. It demonstrates, in our respectful submission, what the spirit of rules is in a wide section of the jurisdictions throughout the world and demonstrates, in our submission, that the evil that is aimed at is to prevent people in authority, police officers, customs offers, whoever it may be, going to someone and getting him to confess by improper means. One of the interesting features of the 1984 Act was this, that it introduced tape recordings of interviews, and that was done specifically with this in mind. That was done to protect not just defendants but also the police officers, against whom numerous allegations were made of various kinds. It's a matter of note that one of the features that this Tribunal has plainly picked up from such a system is Rule 43, which requires the careful recording in a particular way of interviews. I use that as an example to demonstrate the way in which this Tribunal's rules of procedure and evidence are plainly reflective of the kind of procedures that exist in the world outside. As I've said, it gives me no pleasure to criticise the laws of a European nation with which my country enjoys good relations. The fact is, in our respectful submission, that what passes for human rights in that country's criminal procedure falls lamentably far short of the standards which this honourable Tribunal has set. We respectfully submit that to permit the interview with the Austrian police to be admitted would offend quite clearly against rules 95 and 89(d). The second basis on which I respectfully submit that this Tribunal should reject the admissibility of that interview is this. Firstly, it wasn't regrettably audio or video recorded. Secondly, it was conducted with a man who on the evidence of Mr. Moerbauer must have been desperately tired. Your Honours will recall the evidence of Mr. Moerbauer on this point. He admitted that he, who was not the person who was the suspect, was very tired. Your Honours can well imagine that after a day of that kind, where from 2.15 in the afternoon until some time just after midnight Mr. Mucic was put through the various procedures -- and I complain not about him being arrested and I complain not about the fact of his being interviewed -- but the reality was by the time he came to be interviewed and by the time the interview came to an end, your Honours can properly infer from the evidence before you that he must have been a man who was desperately tired. I add this to that, that he was interviewed over a period of some four and three-quarter hours by a total of some five different police officers being in and out of that room. In my respectful submission to have an interview of that length is in itself oppressive. These features alone, the facts that I've just laid before you, and certainly when taken together with what I have described as the breaches of human rights, to which I have adverted, would also on their own be sufficient, in our respectful submission, to cause the exclusion of the interviews. I turn now to linking that interview with the full procedure that was then carried out by the Office of the Prosecution. I make this point. The first is this: we have submitted in our motion that there is a proper cause to consider what might loosely be described as the cross-culture aspect of this procedure. This was a man who comes from part of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Before you proceed further, I just want to know under the English law an accused has a right to have his counsel present when he is being interviewed by the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. I have never been present at a police interview, because that is done in the split --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It's a question of law really. Does the law provide it at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The law makes it plain that he has at all times the right to have his solicitor present at an interview. The solicitor can only be removed if he is misbehaving in some way and that can only be given on the authority of, I think, a Police Superintendent. So in essence his lawyer is entitled to be there at all times if he wants him. Mr. Mucic was a man who plainly came from part of the former Yugoslavia. He is a man who grew up there and will have had all the cultural overlay that such a life would have given him. Plainly he had lived in Austria for quite some time and was no doubt familiar with the street-wise ways of that country, but the fact of the matter is that over a period of four days he was subjected to two quite different cultures, and I have adverted to the way in which the Austrian civil rights differ from the civil rights of this Tribunal. Within a space of four days he was subjected to those two quite distinct systems, which, in my respectful submission, are pretty well opposed to one another in the terms of the kinds of rights that they afford. That leads me then to Mr. Abribat. The Prosecution plainly relies upon him as a witness of fact. What they say is this and what he says is this, that the previous conversation which is referred to at the beginning of his first interview with the Office of the Prosecution, Mr. Abribat claims that that took place in the space of one or two minutes on 18th March 1996. I am going to go, and I hope your Honours will bear with me as I go through the facts that are laid before you -- can I remind you of what my learned friend Ms McHenry said on 14th May of this year? In dealing with this issue about the cross-culture aspect she said this: "The Rules state very clearly that an accused must be informed of his rights and that the accused must knowingly and voluntarily waive those rights". In our respectful submission, that was a concession by the Prosecution that it goes simply beyond someone saying "yes"; that there has to be an informed knowing consent to the issue of: "I'm not going to have a lawyer". I remind your Honours of that, because the Prosecution plainly said that, and I have extracted it from my computer today. Let us just look at what Mr. Abribat had to say. When he was examined-in-chief he said this: "We asked for permission to be in Austria when Mr. Mucic was arrested. There were four of us representatives of the Office of the Prosecution, plus an interpreter". He then goes on to describe the man called Mr. Dutoit and who the investigators were. He describes contacting the authorities in Austria. He was asked this: "Question: On 18th March did you or anyone from the Office of the Prosecutor have any contact with Mr. Mucic? Answer: On the day that he was arrested? On that day all five of us went back to the police station. We had a discussion with the police officer who was responsible for the operation and after the discussion I asked him whether I could meet Mr. Mucic to explain to him who we were and what the procedure would be that could be followed, should he accept to give testimony -- make a statement, rather. Then I asked to see him. Question: What happened, please? Answer: The Austrian police officer said that that was all right. He said that I could come with him as well as the interpreter and that he would let us speak with Mr. Mucic. That is what was done. I went with the police officer and the interpreter. He took us to a kind of cell, like the cells we have in my country, and there I met Mr. Mucic. Question: Can you please tell us what happened when you met Mr. Mucic? Answer: I introduced myself. I told him who I was. I introduced the interpreter and I told him that we were members of the Office of the Prosecutor of the International Tribunal, that there were specific proceedings that were followed at the International Tribunal and that we wished to ask him questions, and that in order to do so we would have to honour the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. That's what it was. I spoke to him for maybe one minute, maybe two minutes". He then describes the language in which he spoke. He says this a bit further on: "There was no real discussion, because I simply came in to see Mr. Mucic and to explain who I was, that is to introduce myself, to explain the rules, and I simply wanted to know whether he agreed or not to be questioned. He answered -- he nodded. Actually, which meant "yes", and that's all". Can I ask your Honours now, as we look at that particular section, to imagine yourself as fresh young lawyers again, seeking to explain to your clients the Rules of Evidence and procedure that are contained in Rules 42 and 43? I invite your Honours to consider this: do you think you could explain them to somebody whose language was different from yours in one or two minutes? I pose that question to invite your Honours to consider whether this witness was actually telling you the truth when he claims to have explained the Rules of Procedure and Evidence to Mr. Mucic. In our respectful submission to try to explain Rules 42 and 43 to someone like Mr. Mucic in a couple of minutes is simply a ludicrous notion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This conversation was not video taped?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And it wasn't video taped. If it had been Mr. Abribat would be able to demonstrate to us what he had done. It is for that reason that I adverted to the introduction in the United Kingdom of tape recording being for the protection of both defendants and police officers and that's why this Tribunal has such rules. It is there to protect the defendant and the investigators. It is there to prevent just this sort of conversation taking place or just the sort of conversation that I alleged to Mr. Abribat had taken place in the 20 minutes that followed the court appearance before Judge Seda and the beginning of the interviews with the Office of the Prosecution. He goes on to describe how the day after the arrest the entire team, that is the five people: "We went to the investigating judge's office in Austria, the person who was in charge of the case. We met him. He explained to us that there would be a discussion with Mr. Mucic in order to tell him that there were extradition proceedings going on and that after that, if possible, we ourselves would proceed to ask the questions, that we wanted to speak. We had asked very specifically that we be the ones to carry out the questioning of Mr. Mucic for the Prosecutor". I make this small point. It is not an enormous point, but it is perhaps unusual to permit one side of an argument to go and talk to the judge before the proceedings start. That in itself offends somewhat against the proprieties of justice. Of course, there are occasions when ex parte applications are made either by prosecutors or by defence counsel, but those are very unusual and they arise in very specific circumstances. To have people going off and chatting to the judge before the defendant is brought up, in the absence of the defendant, offends, in our respectful submission, against any proper notion of open justice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But in your system there are no investigating judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: No, but you shouldn't go talking to judges in the absence of one of the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Investigating judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Of course, but here are people who have no legal standing in Austria talking to an investigating judge. Nothing was told to Mr. Mucic that this conversation has taken place. He goes on to describe how the meeting with Mr. Mucic subsequently took place in front of Judge Seda, with his interpreter, the five members of the team -- their names I have already given you -- from the Office of the Prosecutor: "Mr. Mucic was brought in. The investigating judge spoke with Mr. Mucic. He spoke in German. That was interpreted for Mr. Mucic through the judge's interpreter. We said nothing. We did not participate in that discussion. We simply listened and I asked our translator to give me a synopsis of what the judge was saying to Mr. Mucic. That's how I was able to understand that the judge was apparently explaining the extradition proceeding after which, with his authorisation, we could ourselves question him". It goes on: "If I recall correctly, I followed these things in a really synoptical form, what my interpreter was saying to me. It seemed to me that the Austrian investigating judge must have said to Mr. Mucic that he was entitled or he should insist on his right to having an attorney during the extradition proceedings". Well, I remind your Honour of the questioning of Mr. Abribat as to why he thought he was in Vienna. There was a Rule 40 request, of course, and it's plain, in my respectful submission, that why Mr. Abribat was there, despite his protestations, which your Honours may find extraordinary, protestations to the contrary that he had no idea there were going to be any extradition proceedings and he was not a specialist in extradition -- one wonders why he bothered to go to Vienna at all. The reality is Mr. Abribat knew that one of the purposes of his being there was to try to get him to be extradited at the end of the day and he was part of that process. He goes on to say this. He was asked about what happened at the end of that discussion: "Question: Was there any discussion that you were aware of whether Mr. Mucic wished or should have an attorney with respect to an interview to be conducted by the Office of the Prosecutor as opposed to the extradition proceedings? Answer: No, not at all, from what I remember and I think I do remember things rather well, it was a question of a lawyer but only for the extradition". Your Honour, in my submission what, in fact, the document says is. "I want a lawyer" and that was an expression that he had said not once but twice during the course of that day and also before the learned judge, Judge Ortner. He says this: "It seems to me that the judge must have explained we would then have a hearing but before that took place, if Mr. Mucic wanted a rest, wanted a break before we began -- I think he must have asked him that question because Mr. Mucic did, in fact, say he wanted to have a break before we would begin". He then goes on to describe how the meeting took place. He says this: "The guards must have asked Mr. Mucic to withdraw. We also left the office. The judge told us that we could not use the office we were in because it had to be used for something else".

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down again a little bit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: "I do not really remember what it was, but it had to be used for something else in any case and we would have to go into an adjoining room. It was actually adjoining the office. It could be compared to a kind of place where people speak to prisoners in a prison. It was a narrow room. That's where we went. When I say "we", it means the second investigator of the group, Bart d'Hooge, the interpreter, Peter Nicholson, who was responsible for the recording equipment that we'd brought with us, and myself. So then there were four of us only. The legal expert, Mr. Dutoit, was involved doing other things with the Austrian authorities, so didn't stay with us. We went into that room, as I said, which was right next door. We prepared the recording equipment. That is the tape recorder and the camera. It took us a little bit of time because it was a very small room. We had to find the proper angle where we would be able to take pictures properly. That was not an easy thing to do. Then we waited until Mr. Mucic came back. Question: What happened when Mr. Mucic came? Answer: When Mr. Mucic arrived, he sat down in front of us, and then at that point we began to ask the questions. Question: Can you tell us more exactly what exactly -- when Mr. Mucic entered the room, was the recording equipment already going? Can you just explain exactly how that worked, if any conversation occurred before the recording equipment started? Can you please just tell us about that? Answer: Mr. Mucic arrived. He sat down. I think I said "hello" to him again. I must have shown him the camera and I said to him: "This is the equipment that we're going to use in order to record this hearing. I'm also going to show you the video recording saying "this is the other piece of equipment we are going to use" and we will respect the forms that I gave to you yesterday". I said to him: "We can begin when you want". He must have said "all right" and then we began. Question: When you said what happened then, was the recording equipment turned on? Answer: From the point on that he said "all right", that is from the point that he agreed to our recording what he said, we started the equipment and I again told him what point we were at, who was there. I don't exactly recall all the legal forms that I had. Do you want me to repeat exactly what they were, these legal forms, as saying what was said at that point?" He then describes that. In cross-examination he said this about the meeting he had held with Mr. Mucic the day before: "I explained the procedure in English so that the Austrian police officer could understand me, but the texts are worded in English and in French". He goes on: "I wanted to explain the Rules of Procedure that applied in questioning a suspect and then on that basis to know whether he would agree to an interview". He denied wanting to ask him any questions and said that he had been clear on that. "I simply wanted to explain the Rules of Procedure, and I didn't enter into any dialogue with him". He said this in answer to my question, which was this: "Question: Did you ask him the question: "Do you want a lawyer?" Answer: No, I did not put that question to him. I explained the Rules of Procedure of the Tribunal to him and told him the conditions in which and circumstances in which he could have a lawyer." I pose this question to your Honours: if he never asked him the question: "Do you want a lawyer?", how could he possibly have known at the beginning of the interview that Mr. Mucic didn't want a lawyer? The answer is this: he did know that Mr. Mucic didn't want a lawyer because he had had a conversation with him about that very subject in the 20 minute period before the interview began, because he plainly did not ask him in the only other conversation he had with him, because that's the evidence he has given to the court, so there must have been another conversation in which Mr. Abribat did ask him about wanting a lawyer. That can only have been in the period of 20 minutes between Judge Seda ending his hearing and the interview beginning. I want your Honours to remember that piece of evidence. I'll repeat it. I asked him this question: "Question: did you ask him the question: "Do you want a lawyer?" Answer: No, I did not put that question to him". In our respectful submission, that is a crucial piece of evidence and it goes to undermine the Prosecution's case that nothing untoward happened. In our respectful submission something thoroughly untoward did happen, and I would invite your Honours to reject Mr. Abribat's evidence on the point of what happened and, indeed, Mr. d'Hooge on the point of what happened in the 20 minutes between 15:10 hours and 15:30 hours on 19th March. He's not telling you the truth. Something did happen. I suggested to him that he was effectively brow-beating Mr. Mucic into having interviews without a lawyer. It's quite extraordinary, isn't it, that here was a man, Mr. Mucic, who throughout the hearings before the Austrian judges was saying: "I want a lawyer", and then suddenly he turns round and says: "All right. I'm happy not to have a lawyer". It's quite extraordinary, in our respectful submission, that that should take place without anything being done or said to him. We respectfully submit that something did happen in those 20 minutes, something which Mr. Abribat has concealed from your Honours, and that the only possible and proper inference to draw from the evidence I have laid before you is that something did take place, and it was oppressive, and it was designed to get him to agree not to have a lawyer. I will not bore your Honours by going on at great length about the rest of the evidence. It's a matter of note that Mr. Abribat seemed unable to recall, as your Honours will remember, Rule 42(B) and Judge Karibi Whyte will remember having an exchange with me about that very topic. Your Honour said this, that that should have been explained to Mr. Mucic. Mr. Abribat seemed unable to remember that that was part of Rule 42. In our submission, the evidence of Mr. Abribat, when examined carefully, simply ultimately undoes the Prosecution's case when they say that this was voluntarily and knowingly a waiver of his right to counsel. Would your Honour just give me a moment, please? During the course of his cross-examination he said this, that in relation to whether or not Mr. Mucic wanted a lawyer he said: "I didn't get a full translation". In our respectful submission, something that this man should have done is to inform himself properly and fully of what was being said to the learned judge and to make sure that he was properly aware of what it was Mr. Mucic desired. He failed to do so and, in our respectful submission, he failed in a way that undermines the process that was conducted. He should have enquired properly what it was that Mr. Mucic wanted a lawyer for and have satisfied himself before interviewing him that this was a waiver, if waiver it was, that was knowingly and freely given. This point was put to him, that he was exceptionally keen to interview this man. Your Honours may think there is a good reason for that, and you will recall from your days in practice that if you can get a man whilst he is in the first moments of confusion and worry at being arrested, if you can get him to talk at that time, you are doing very well, and you will always get something out of someone. There was no need to hurry along into interviews with Mr. Mucic. An indictment was in the stage of preparation and it was signed on the 19th and confirmed on the 21st. There had been a provisional request under Rule 40. There was every likelihood that this man was going to be transferred promptly here to The Hague, where all the facilities would exist and the rules exist to permit interviews. It could have been done at great leisure rather than in the uncomfortable surroundings of this tiny room. Your Honours may want to ask this question of yourselves: why should there be this almost indecent haste to interview this man? Was it because they knew if he got a lawyer in, that might get this man to clam up and they wouldn't get anything out of him and that's why they were so keen to persuade him not to have a lawyer? I ask your Honours to look at that point and wonder why it is they should have had this urgent desire to interview him, when there was every likelihood they could have done it in more comfortable surroundings and at greater leisure here in the Hague. Can I now turn to the evidence of Mr. Gschwendt, whom you will recall was -- I think his rank was Captain or Hauptmann from the Austrian police. He was unable to assist Mr. Abribat in any way as to the nature of the conversation that had been conducted with him. Your Honours will recall the evidence of the Austrian police that essentially Mr. Mucic was kept in Room 331. Mr. Abribat claims to have spoken to him in a cell and had this one or two minute explanation of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence in a cell. Your Honours will have to look at that and decide whether Mr. Abribat was being entirely truthful with you when he says that's where he conducted this conversation. Captain Gschwendt is unable, as he says, to reconstruct the conversation, so that the only person upon whom you could begin to place any reliance as to the truth or otherwise of what he says is Mr. Abribat himself. In my respectful submission, for the reasons that I have identified, Mr. Abribat is not a witness upon whom you can rely as being either honest or accurate. I will not go on about Mr. Moerbauer. His evidence has been very recent, and your Honours will recall it. What it comes to is this, we say. Firstly, when you take the whole procedure together you have a situation where the first interview by the Austrian police was one which was procured by means which were in breach of his human rights, and there is then the argument that what was subsequently done becomes the fruit of the poisoned tree, to use a well-worn phrase. In our respectful submission, taking all these factors together, the cross-cultural aspect, the evidence that I have adverted to in this case, the only proper conclusion that this honourable Tribunal can come to is that all these interviews were, in fact, obtained in breach of Rule 95, and this court must take what I appreciate will be a bold decision, but must say to itself: "The Prosecution has not proved beyond reasonable doubt that Mr. Mucic knowingly and voluntarily waived his right to counsel. The Prosecution has not proved beyond reasonable doubt that the interview with the Austrian police was free and fair", and if that be right, the Defence of Mr. Mucic says this: the only proper course is to say: "We exclude this evidence and we exclude it because it's in breach of Rule 95 and Rule 89(D)". Are there any other matters upon which I can assist any of your Honours? Those are my submissions in support of the motion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me note some things as a preliminary matter. One is that I am not repeat everything that is in the Prosecution's response to Mr. Mucic's motion. We believe it was a lengthy response, which discusses in some length the law, the fact and what we submit is the appropriate analysis. So, like my learned colleague, I will not repeat those, but I will rely on them in the assumption that your Honours have read them. Also preliminarily we will note that we, the Prosecution, do not agree that the standard here is beyond a reasonable doubt. We think that is incorrect under the rules of this Tribunal and under the Tadic decisions, but in any event we will just note that even were that the standard, it is absolutely clear that these statements, in particular the Office of the Prosecutor's statement that we are discussing now, would meet that and any other standard. I will briefly discuss just -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Let us get this clear before we go on. Is it your submission that the proof of voluntariness is not beyond reasonable doubt?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour. I know different systems have different standards and, for instance, I do understand that from where Mr. Greaves comes from that is the standard. It is not in the United States. I believe under the rules of this Tribunal and under the Tadic Decision with respect to admission of evidence that is not the relevant standard. It is, of course, the relevant standard for guilt. Let me be very clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I was not given a copy of the information sheet. I do not have a copy of the information sheet which the Austrian police made Mr. Mucic to sign before recording his statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I believe it's part of the record in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Do you have the English translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I am afraid mine is marked in all sorts of ways that I would not like your Honour to see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I know. It contains your notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: It is attached as Annexe 3 to my learned friend's motion. It may be you can derive it from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours. I can provide your Honours with a copy of it. It is annex 3. I believe the witness, Mr. Gschwendt, identified the German original. Here is another copy. I will briefly discuss just for a minute, because my colleague, Mr. Greaves did, the Austrian interview. As your Honours know, the Prosecution has offered previously to make submissions about both Austrian law and specifics about how, in fact, the Austrian statement should be admitted. Your Honours have deferred ruling on that, but because Mr. Greaves has discussed it in some length, I will briefly respond and again renew the Prosecution's offer to have Mr. Stefan Waespi, who is much more knowledgeable about both Austrian law and, in fact, international -- and how that is in accordance with all of the human rights conventions and human -- fundamental human rights in detail, but now I would just like to briefly respond, and if your Honours want further --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I just want to ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We are not bound by any national rules in this investigation. The standard of -- what should I say -- the grounds which have to be given to the accused before he makes a statement can be spelled out from Rule 42. Even though a statement may be admissible under a national system, are we bound to accept it if it doesn't come up to the standards of Rule 42 of our rules?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I believe that your Honours may certainly accept statements --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It may be admissible in the Austrian courts, but are we bound to accept it if it doesn't come up to the standards of Rule 42? That's the question I want to ask.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, my response is whether or not it is or is not admissible in an Austrian court is entirely not controlling for this court. So the fact that we believe that it would be is not controlling, but even if it were not admissible, we believe that would not be controlling. We believe what's controlling is Rule 95. We believe Rule 42 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You haven't got my -- probably I have not been able to make you understand. Rule 42 lays down the standards. These are the precautions which the suspect is to be informed of or the precautions which are to be taken. If a statement is recorded by police, although admissible under a national system, we do not criticise that national system at all, but if a statement does not come up to the standard laid down by our own rules, are we bound to admit it into evidence just because it is admissible in evidence under a national system?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I do understand, your Honour. I am afraid I am the one who is not being clear and you are. You are certainly not bound to accept it just because it is admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I am not criticising any system.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I understand that, your Honour. Without criticising or not criticising any particular system, the Prosecution's submission is that you are not bound by the fact that a statement would be admissible in a national court. The Prosecution would argue, however, that Rule 42 does not control interviews taken by non-Tribunal -- by persons other than the Office of the Prosecutor, and that Rule 42 is not the appropriate standard for evaluating statements taken by other systems. The appropriate standard is Rule 95, which was the information, was the evidence, in this case a statement of an accused, was it taken into violation of fundamental human rights, or would its admission somehow seriously affect the integrity of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Standards of fundamental rights differ from state to state. In some states the standards are much higher. In other states the standards are not so high. So the standards really don't count. The question is whether a statement which does not come up to the criteria laid down by our Rule would be admissible in evidence before us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution certainly would agree that standards differ in all kinds of different systems, but I believe that is why your Honours adopted Rule 95, which states that you are not bound either positively or neglect difficulty by any national law, including admission of evidence, or even how they take it, but that it is accepted that there are some fundamental rights which will control and which are a minimum, as well as anything that would seriously undermine the integrity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You see, for example, in my country any statement made by an accused person before the police is inadmissible in evidence. So that's a different standard altogether. When we come to an International Tribunal we have to have the standards which are laid down by our own rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's right. I think the only thing that we differ -- that it appears we may differ on is that the Prosecution believes that the appropriate standard is that set out in Rule 95, and your Honour seems to be suggesting that the appropriate standard is Rule 42.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Maybe I'm just doing a little louting (sic), nothing more than that. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Let me get this fairly straight. Wouldn't you agree that any interviews which could be accepted in proceedings in this Tribunal should be able to pass the test of Rule 42?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No, your Honour. We believe that there may well be evidence, including statements of an accused, which do not meet the requirements of Rule 42, for any number of reasons, including that a system is different, but were still fundamentally fair. The fact that we often -- and I will state that, for instance, I believe in Tadic there was an interview taken of Mr. Tadic in the German courts that was admitted and I do not believe that all the requirements of Rule -- I cannot speak to that, but I believe that when you have another system, it is not possible for the exact same rules to always apply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: My fear is that Rule 42 can be easily bypassed by not recording the statement and instead only producing the statement recorded under the national system and national laws. Rule 42 can be bypassed easily.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may well be that in certain cases where your Honour -- I'm sorry -- where it appears that the Office of the Prosecutor has intentionally tried to circumvent the requirements of Rule 42 by relying on a national system, that that -- that your Honours would determine that that somehow fundamentally offended the integrity of these proceedings where there's any sort of suggestion that the Prosecution intentionally manipulated the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I do not say they have done it but it can be done. Rule 42 can be easy bypassed just relying on the statement recorded by the local police. That's my fear.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Then I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I'm sure it will not be done by the Prosecution because you are very honest people, because you are more interested in upholding the justice, but I say it is possible to bypass Rule 42 by not recording a statement of your own and merely relying on the statement recorded by the national police under their national laws.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If your Honours found that the circumstances under which a statement was taken in another system were offensive in terms of this Tribunal's notions of fairness and integrity, certainly your Honours would have the authority and even the duty to exclude it. What the Prosecution is submitting is that in this case and in many cases before this Tribunal people are arrested in other places where different systems must apply, and different places have their own interest in obtaining evidence quite appropriately, and they follow their own system, as they are required to do, and the issue is: does it somehow -- was it fundamentally unfair rather than to specifically always read out Rule 95 or not and with respect -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: But isn't it the reason why we are not bound by national systems when, in fact, national systems might even offend against our own rules?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: That is why we are not bound by it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That's exactly right, your Honour. That's why I believe Rule 95 was explicitly set out. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I suppose it could be, but except perhaps you tie yourself down with the definition of who is a Prosecutor under Rule 42. That's where the interview is done by you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That is right. I believe the definition of Prosecutor is set out in the definitions. The Prosecutor is defined in your Honours' Rules -- the Rules of this Tribunal as: "The Prosecutor refers to the Prosecutor appointed pursuant to Article 16 of the Statute". So we certainly agree that Rules 42 and 43 apply to all interviews taken by the Prosecutor or the Office of the Prosecutor. That's right. JUDGE ODIO BENITO: To be clear, but only in that case, because we have the Article 18 of the Statute that stated the right of the suspect, paragraph 3. So according to your opinion we should understand that if questioned, it's by the Prosecution only.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We believe that's clear from the entire reading of the Rule, even if it doesn't in every single case where it talks about it state the Prosecutor and we believe that's the correct interpretation and it is clarified by the exact wording of Rule 42. JUDGE ODIO BENITO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So the fact that Austrian law is not controlling is why, in fact, the Prosecutor has not had and does not intend to provide your Honours with specifics about what Austrian law is and is not, because we believe it's not relevant. What's relevant is: was the interview taken fairly, and again I will emphasise that what we were talking about here is not about the admission of the Austrian statement, because your Honours have postponed that, but only about the Office of the Prosecutor interview, but I feel constrained just to say a few remarks about the Austrian interview, because my learned colleague has said that that was so offensive that it somehow taints everything else that has, and so the Prosecution must respond. In fact, in its submission there was nothing offensive about anything that happened in the Austrian interview. The accused was advised that he could consult with an attorney, including before deciding whether or not to give an interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just a moment. Now you are talking about the interview recorded by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am talking about the Austrian interview. Since Mr. Greaves has indicated that it was so offensive that it taints the Office of the Prosecutor interview, I am just going to briefly respond to that, because the Office of the Prosecutor does not believe that anything that happened in the Austrian interview was offensive, and in a minute I'll also talk about how it also doesn't -- no matter what happened, it doesn't taint the Office of the Prosecutor interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just a minute. We don't intend to criticise the Austrian system at all. We are just wondering. It might be said we are saying the Austrian system is against fundamental rights. We are not criticising the system.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I understand that your Honours are not saying that. I believe, and I believe my learned colleague Mr. Greaves would agree with this, Mr. Greaves believes it does. That is one of the basis for his arguments. Even though your Honours have not suggested, and I do not think anyone has interpreted anything your Honours have said to criticise the Austrian system, because Mr. Greaves has, I just want to briefly speak to it. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: What the rules say is we are not bound. It does not mean that we cannot take it into account.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That is exactly right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: For our purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: It may well be that national system are often instructive or helpful. I do not mean to suggest that at all, in fact. That is why I am going to briefly discuss Austrian law just for a minute in response to Mr. Greaves, if I may. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I mention that so that you can see the relevance of the argument of Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I believe that, as opposed to the searches, that even Mr. Greaves agrees that Austrian law was complied with, with respect to the interview of the accused, and Austrian law provides -- and everyone agrees that this happened in this case -- that Mr. Mucic was advised that he had the right to consult with an attorney and he chose not to do so. It is also the case that under Austrian law, and Mr. Mucic was informed of this, you do not have the right to have your lawyer present during questioning. We note that that is the case in many, many countries, including in many European countries other than Austria, and this has consistently been found to be in accordance with fundamental human rights, including the European convention of human rights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just a minute. What is the position -- in England Mr. Greaves said a lawyer can be present. What is the position in the United States?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is the case, your Honour, in the United States that the accused has the right to have an attorney present when he is questioned. I will note that my understanding, and I am not an expert in Austrian law or in the United Kingdom law, and we can supply, if your Honours wish it, more details later, but I don't -- I believe that there are certain circumstances in the United Kingdom where an accused is not permitted to have his counsel present. In fact, I believe that in a recent case in the European Court of Human Rights, the case was Murray V United Kingdom, a judgement of 8th February 1996 in the Human Rights Law Journal, 1996, pages 39-51, and under this the Criminal Evidence Order of 1988, which I believe is applicable to Northern Ireland says that an accused's right to counsel may be delayed for 48 hours. An accused in that case was interviewed ten times without having the opportunity to talk to his attorney and the European Court found that was not impermissible under the European Convention on Human Rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I hate to interrupt my learned friend and I don't wish to disturb the flow of her argument which I am listening to with great care. In fact, that legislation is particularly aimed at terrorist offences. It is in particular circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: There may be particular circumstances in the United Kingdom where an accused is not permitted to have his counsel present. That has been found to be in accordance with fundamental human rights, including the European Convention. So the fact that Austria has this we do not believe somehow makes the Austrian interview offensive to fundamental human rights. The second issue Mr. Greaves spoke to was the idea that he is telling someone, in addition to telling them they do not have to speak, but if they do give a confession, such could be considered mitigating evidence, the idea of telling someone who is accurate, what is, in fact, the law, that that constitutes improper inducement the Prosecution finds simply unacceptable. Certainly the police are entitled to tell people and arguably should tell the people both sides. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Let me not interrupt your train of thought. You mean if somebody is asked to confess, or agree with doing what you did not do, that is a good way of saying the person is telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I do not suggest that if someone is told they should confess regardless of the truth of the matter that that would not be a problem, but the Prosecution strongly suggest that as part of advising someone of their rights that they are advised that they should speak truthfully and that if they are subsequently convicted, a confession could constitute mitigating evidence, that although it may not be usual in some countries, where an accused may, in fact, be encouraged not to speak, there is absolutely nothing wrong with it and one could argue it is appropriate such that an accused has the correct information in front of him and if something the accused could do at this time could later be considered mitigating evidence, there is nothing improper with telling him that because at the same time the accused is told: "You don't have to speak and obviously what you speak may later hurt or help you". The Prosecution doesn't believe that there can be any argument that telling someone who is uncontroversial, what is clearly correct law, could constitute somehow improper inducement. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In the context of a confession what would be the inducement -- in the context of a confession what would be an inducement? Something telling him if he makes a statement he will be able to avoid some pain, some loss in property or in person?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Certainly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: If you tell him you will gain by making an a confession, isn't it an inducement?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: You are not telling the accused he will gain. At the same time you are telling the accused whatever he says may be used against him. To say: "If you tell the truth, it may later help you" the Prosecution believes is absolutely fair. It's not as if he was told -- Mr. Greaves mentioned some arguments that had been found improper, such as: "If you confess we won't go arrest your wife" or something like that, but the issue is: is something an improper inducement? The fact that by talking someone is able to give their side of the story or if they are later convicted that it would constitute mitigating evidence, the Prosecution thinks there can be nothing, nothing improper about telling someone what the law is, so that they are entitled to make the decision, because there may be many circumstances where it is -- if an accused is convicted, that his confession will be used as mitigating evidence, and he may wish to have that information while he makes his decision: "Should I talk or should I not?" The final issue raised by Mr. Greaves is that Mr. Mucic was tired, and the Prosecution believes that the evidence does support that Mr. Mucic was tired, but the Prosecution does not believe that that means that there was anything improper in continuing the interview. Mr. Mucic was told he did not have to speak and Mr. Mucic could have stopped the interview any time he wanted. Arrested persons may often be tired. We may often be tired. The issue is: are you unable to make rational decisions or somehow otherwise unable to think? The Prosecution believes there is no evidence that Mr. Mucic was in such a state. To the contrary, a review of his statement shows that he was in full control of his faculties at all time. An accused can always state they're tired and they may often be tired, but the issue is: was the accused in control of his faculties, and the Prosecution suggests that the evidence overwhelmingly shows that he was. If anything, the fact that he may have been tired goes to the weight rather than the admissibility of his statement. The Prosecution would now like to go to what we consider at this particular point the actual relevant issue, which is the Office of the Prosecutor interview. We would point out that the Office of the Prosecutor interview was entirely separate from the Austrian police interview. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Please. I think that is what really gives me some anxiety, the continuity between the two interviews and the different, inconsistent warnings. That gives me anxiety. If you can --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is the case that with this Tribunal every accused is going to be at various points faced with different legal systems, and the issue is: was there some sort of unfair or improper confusion, and in this case the Prosecution believes it is very clear that the two were always treated as separate entities, and that the accused, Mr. Mucic, understood them as separate. We will point out in this regard that the Austrian police were not present at the Office of the Prosecutor interview. Similarly, the Office of the Prosecutor interviewers were not present for the Austrian interviews. The proceedings were different. They were different persons, they were different places, they were different times. Most importantly, the procedure for each was clearly explained to the accused. If the accused was confused he may have chosen to try to speak to an attorney, but he chose not to. The rights were very clearly on numerous occasions told to Mr. Mucic, and the Prosecution believes the evidence is clear that he did understand that they were different proceedings. That's why one of the reasons the Prosecution believes Rule 42 is so strict is because there are going to be different systems, and there should not be unfair confusion about the governing rules. In this case that's why the accused was, I believe, on six different occasions all tape recorded advised of his rights under the Tribunal. He was advised by the Tribunal people, in a Tribunal interview with no one else. It was explained to him at the beginning that these were people from the members of the Office of the Prosecutor. The Prosecution believes that the fact that there were two different interviews does not mean that somehow the accused could not understand what is very clearly set out to him. I will then go on. The relevant persons who gave evidence about the Office of the Prosecutor interview and the circumstances leading up to it were Lieutenant Gschwendt, Mr. Abribat and Mr. d'Hooge. Starting again responding to Mr. Greaves, Mr. Greaves points out on the 18th Mr. Abribat for a few minutes met with Mr. Mucic to introduce himself and to give him an overview of the rules and see if he wanted to potentially give an interview. Given the circumstances and the fact that Mr. Mucic did not have to give an interview, given the fact that the Austrian authorities did not have to permit an interview, it was an entirely reasonable thing to find out if -- to introduce themselves and give Mr. Mucic a very brief description of who they were and what they wished to discuss with him, which was whether or not he would be willing to give an interview. Mr. Gschwendt and Mr. Abribat both were present and discussed this. Mr. Gschwendt testified that Mr. Mucic was in the cell, including for discussion, at various times, that the Office of the Prosecutor did talk to him, that Mr. Gschwendt monitored the conversation, that he did not remember the words or the exact substance of what was discussed, but he could say and he did say explicitly that there was nothing improper or any kind of oppression, and then that was his job, to make sure that that did not occur, and he stated very clearly that that did not occur. Mr. Abribat also explained it in great detail in examination. Mr. Greaves points out that Mr. Abribat said he met with him for a brief period of time. Mr. Abribat never said that he read out every single word, and it may be the case that Mr. Abribat miscalculated by the couple of minutes how long the interview took, but the Prosecution does not believe there can be any argument that any sort of unfair oppression or anything improper occurred. The two witnesses with information about that have testified clearly and convincingly exactly what happened. Then we go to, in fact, what is the allegation of oppression, which is this 20 minutes. The Prosecution will point out that there is absolutely no evidence whatsoever in support of this allegation. This allegation, which was made over a year later by the accused, which we do think is relevant, has been shown to be totally and utterly groundless. In fact, what has been testified to by both Mr. Abribat and Mr. d'Hooge is that during this 20 minutes Mr. Mucic was taken away by the guards for a rest, and that they set up the equipment in another room in Mr. Mucic's absence and when Mr. Mucic was back in, about 20 minutes later, he's asked if he agrees that the interview be recorded. It's agreed and then the interview starts. When I say the interview starts, though, in fact, what happens is Mr. Mucic is very carefully explained his rights. There's no challenge to this. It's in the recording. An accused is always going to be able to say: "Something happened before" and unless you tape an accused 24 hours a day from the moment he's arrested, there's no way to establish that other than the testimony of the persons who had contact with him, which we've done, but it's very clear that Mr. Mucic was treated fairly and was given his rights, because in the beginning of the interview he explained every single right and asked does he want to give an interview, does he wish to have an attorney, and he indicates that he is willing to give an interview without an attorney. The idea that somehow on the basis of absolutely no evidence this court should disregard the testimony of all the witnesses whom we believe the court must find credible when you take into account what they said, their demeanour, everything, is, we think, just utterly lacking in possibility or merit. In fact, we will point out that during this interview, which occurred over three days for a few hours a day, large breaks in between, Mr. Mucic is read his rights, I believe, at least six times. Every time he indicates he wants to continue without an attorney he is asked if he wants to continue the interview and told he doesn't have to continue it if he doesn't want to. He says: "Yes, I want to continue". If there's any question about what happened or Mr. Mucic's demeanour -- your Honour, Mr. Mucic just made a kissing signal to me which he's now confirming. I would ask that he be directed not to make such --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Mr. Greaves, this is not on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I quite agree, your Honours. I have indicated my displeasure to Mr. Mucic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This is intimidating counsel and this is contempt of court.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: He will not do it again. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I hope they should learn to leave their indiscipline from outside and when they come in here they should try to be disciplined. They might have been so used to indiscipline elsewhere. It should not be so here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. If there's any question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I have a few questions really. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: The Trial Chamber will now break for 30 minutes and we will come back. (11.30 am). (Short break)

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honours, before we resume hearing from my learned friend Ms. McHenry could I just say this on behalf of my client, he understands that he overstepped the mark this morning. He did not mean any disrespect to your Honours and apologises if any disrespect was felt by your Honours. I am sure you will all understand it is quite stressful to be sitting there for hours on end and sometimes bad judgement is arrived at by a defendant. He apologises to your Honours for it and I hope your Honours accept the apology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The apology should be to Ms McHenry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: He and I have had a conversation about it and I am confident it will not happen again. I hope that draws the matter to a close. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I will seize this opportunity to say a few things. I haven't been watching the behaviour of the accused persons, because I have never thought it was necessary, and knowing the gravity for the offences for which they are being tried here, I assumed everybody would behave very soberly and seriously.
