I do not think the general behaviour of accused persons that I have been told of very recently is very much to be desired, and I do not think they appreciate that they can be removed if their conduct interferes with the administration of justice here, and I think they are all reasonable people and they should understand that we give them the due respect they deserve and in reciprocity they should also extend that same respect to every person exercising any duty in this place. Please I appeal to all of them from now to behave very properly and not attract the Trial Chamber to use the law against them. Thank you. Thank you very much, Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's my pleasure, as always.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Ms McHenry, no part of the interview was recorded on 18th March.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour. There was not an interview on 18th March. All there was was a brief introduction of the OTP investigator, Mr. Abribat, and telling him that they wished to seek an interview with him under the rules of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Is it possible to play that portion of the tape from 19th March when the rights of the accused were explained -- the rights of Mucic explained to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Only that portion I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I would suggest, if your Honours would be willing, is that I finish my argument. I just have a couple of minutes left. Part of this suggests that if there's any question about Mr. Mucic and his ability to understand as well as what was told to him, we can play the tape in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I am only interested in that portion: it won't be more than five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: It won't be more than five minutes. I will, of course, point out to your Honours that he was advised of his rights in addition to the first time, I think five other occasions, all of which were also recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I'm only interested in 19th March, that portion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. On 19th, certainly, and I will ask the assistance of the technical persons. I believe the Registrar -- maybe the technical people can get a copy of it from the registrar since it has been identified and while I finish my argument, it can be set up to play the first few minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Another thing I was interested in was what is really the position of the investigating judge in the continental system or Austrian system? Is he a part of the prosecution? I am not really clear about the position of the investigating judge in the system.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will just very briefly respond and then I believe my colleague Mr. Ostberg can either supplement or correct me if I'm wrong. The investigating judge is neither a member of the Prosecution or the Defence. It is a neutral investigator who can interview the accused as, in fact, he did in this case, without the presence of the Prosecutor and also talk to witnesses, and that it is a person who is assigned to investigate an allegation and then at the end of it if he decides that formal charges should be brought, they are brought, and then the person goes before a judicial person for the purposes of determining the person's guilt or innocence rather than the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: To that I would just add that I think it's a fair description to call an investigating judge a judicial supervisor the investigation done by the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to briefly conclude, in addition to pointing out, as I just did, all the different ways in which the Austrian and the Office of the Prosecutor proceedings were kept separate and explained to the accused separately, with respect to the idea that there is confusion because of the different background of the accused and the fact that he is arrested in one country, I'll point out to your Honours that Mr. Delalic -- the Defence of Mr. Delalic made those exact same arguments in its initial motion to exclude the statement of Mr. Delalic, which was taken in Germany, and there was discussion about Yugoslav and German law, and the Chamber, we believe quite correctly, found that given that the Office of the Prosecutor's rules were followed and that the rules of the Tribunal were very clearly explained to him, the allegations about -- indeed, the fact that the accused may also have different legal systems does not render the OTP interview somehow unfair or improper. In addition to playing the first five minutes of this tape, we will again point out that on numerous occasions the accused over a period of three days was explained his rights. He had the opportunity to clarify, if he was confused, to think about it, to change his mind. He specifically was told he can change his mind and does not need to continue. We believe that the idea that he did not understand those rights was frankly entirely baseless. We will point out something that really has not been made much of. The idea that the accused was confused about his desire for an attorney and that he really wanted one is clearly put to rest by the fact that an attorney does appear and, in fact, talks privately to Mr. Mucic, and then both the attorney and Mr. Mucic state: "Mr. Mucic does not want an attorney here as part of the Office of the Prosecutor interview". He may well have wanted one and he did request and get one for the purposes of the extradition proceedings, but he did not want one for the Office of the Prosecutor interviewer, as is made very clear by the fact that he on six or more different occasions waived his right to counsel, by the fact that even when the attorney shows up he says he doesn't want the attorney there. We believe that this answers any possible issue that there might be --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I stand to be corrected but, in fact, there is no evidence before the court that such a conversation took place. Having read it in the Prosecution's response, I was waiting for such evidence to be given. None was given of that conversation. It's, therefore, not in evidence before your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I do believe and we can check the transcript afterwards, and if I'm incorrect, I will -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Actually who is Dr. Manfred?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, there was evidence that an attorney came and that the attorney said he had been appointed to the court for the extradition, that the attorney had -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: That was Dr. Manfred.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That the attorney had a chance to consult with Mr. Mucic privately and the attorney then informed Mr. d'Hooge that Mr. Mucic did not want him, and this was reflected in the record when the interview continued, that Mr. Mucic, in fact, did not wish the attorney present.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: There was plainly evidence as to the arrival of somebody called Dr. Manfred, but my recollection is, and I stand to be corrected, that there was nothing of the conversation that was held with that person was given in evidence. I'm perfectly prepared to be corrected. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: What I do remember is that Dr. Manfred appeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: That is plainly right. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: And finally told them he was leaving because Mr. Mucic did not want him. He didn't need him. That was what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Apparently if my prior argument I was incorrect when I stated that Mr. Gschwendt had testified that Mr. Mucic was both in the room and the arrest cell. That was Mr. Moerbauer who said that. I just wanted to correct that. So, your Honour, we believe that the record is very clear that Mr. Mucic did not want an attorney, despite being not only told he could have one but by having one appear. As was his right to do, he chose not to have one. The Office of the Prosecutor behaved reasonably, appropriately and in every case in accordance with the rules of this Tribunal, as well as any fundamental notions of fairness. It would be, we believe, entirely unjust to allow unsupported allegations of oppression or anything else to result in this statement not being admitted into evidence. Under Rule 42, under Rule 89, which provides that this court shall admit relevant evidence unless it is substantially outweighed by the need to have a fair trial, and under Rule 95 we believe it is very clear that this Office of the Prosecutor interview must be admitted into evidence. At this time I would just ask the technical people to play the beginning portion of the first few minutes of Mr. Mucic's interview on March 19th, which has been identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Before we do that and before my learned friend sits down, could I ask her to deal with this, so that your Honours can hear her response to it? Given the evidence of Mr. Abribat about this: "Question: Did you ask him the question: "Do you want a lawyer?" Answer: No, I did not put that question to him", when does she say -- and the evidence discloses the conversation which is adverted to at the beginning of his evidence, when does she say that conversation took place according to the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution believes that the evidence suggests that after having been advised of his rights Mr. Mucic is asked if he is willing to give an interview under the conditions explained to him and he says "yes". I believe when you read Mr. Abribat's testimony as a whole, he doesn't say that he went through one by one and asked with respect to each question: "Do you understand this? Do you agree to this?" Because all that was to be done the next day on the record. This was just a brief introduction to determine whether or not the efforts to ensure that the Austrian authorities agreed to this, that Mr. Mucic agreed, and that the equipment could be set up, that that is what the conversation alluded to and I believe Mr. Abribat stated that explicitly in his testimony. Thank you. Then I would just ask for the first few minutes of the tape recording to be admitted -- to be shown. (Videotape played).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Excuse me. Can we have the English translation while we watch?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that it be stopped. Yes, your Honour. I don't think the interpretation section was prepared for this. So if your Honours want, maybe -- I believe your Honours have copies of the transcript, but we can also, if we have a couple of minutes, give a copy to the interpretation section and then they can read it. I would just also enquire whether or not your Honours want the translation to be from the French to English or the Serbo-Croatian to English. I would suggest the Serbo-Croatian since what is said to the accused is the most relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: In that case we can either take just a couple of minutes while we give copies of this to the booth or, Mr. Greaves -- I do not know if your Honours want to wait until the end of any suggestion. Otherwise maybe the Registrar can help with providing copies to the interpretation booth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: My difficulty is I don't understand French. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: We can continue while that arrangement is being made.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Mr. Greaves, you can carry on while the arrangement is being made. When it is concluded we can then switch the video on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. There are just a number of matters I want to raise very shortly. I don't accept the proposition that is laid before you concerning the burden of proof in that case. We submit the burden of proof lies on the Prosecution throughout and the standard of proof in this Tribunal is beyond reasonable doubt. The second matter is this: the nature of the attack on Austrian law really derives from the position that Rule 95 throws up, which is to invite the court to look at reliability. That's the test in essence from the Rule, and indeed we would respectfully submit from the decision in Tadic, which we have referred to many times before, which sets out, as it were, the foundation of all evidence has to be reliability. That's the subject that your Honours have in our respectful submission to focus upon in determining the admissibility of these statements: has the Prosecution laid proper ground for reliability and are there features of what happens and the nature of the warnings that are given -- sorry -- the information that's given to suspects that underline the issue of reliability as far as that evidence it concerned? Can I now turn to the case of Murray v United Kingdom? I would be anxious that your Honours have a copy of the actual decision before you rely on it, because the bible that counsel in England all use, Archbold, has a short section on Murray v United Kingdom. It has a slightly different cast upon it and so without seeing the decision, in itself it might be dangerous to rely on, with great respect to my learned friend. What it says here at paragraph 15-225a of the 1997 edition is: "In the context of legislation which permits adverse inferences to be drawn from silence, the right to consult a solicitor is of paramount importance". It then cites Murray v United Kingdom, the 1996 case. Then it says: "Delaying access to legal advice, whatever the justification, is incompatible with the right to a fair trial guaranteed by Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights". So there may be some dispute as to what the precise meaning of Murray is. Having read one or two of the European Court's decisions on various aspects, they can sometimes be slightly elliptical. I notice my learned friend smiles. I think she may have had occasionally the same difficulty that I have had. The next point is this. There is an interesting phrase which is used by the defendant during the course of what he says that he's prepared to do. Can I refer your Honours to it? At page 5 of the Prosecution response they set out the words that are recorded as having been said by the defendant before Judge Seda. At paragraph 12, which ends on page 5, he says this: "I am prepared to meet with investigators of the ICTY and provide them with information". Can I remind your Honours what he did in August of last year, which was to go and provide them with information. That was the interview that was thrown up by my learned friend, my leading counsel. That's what he was trying to do in that interview. Does that indicate, your Honours, how he perceived what the process was that he was about to go through? He thought he was going to give them information. He was under an illusion about that, because what the office of the Prosecution were going to do was to interview him with a view, no doubt, to getting evidence that they could use against him. So is that an indication of someone who has not actually understood what is going to happen to him? Finally this. Again reading that very same paragraph, paragraph 12 of the Prosecution's response, which sets out what happens before Judge Seda, your Honours will see that throughout that there are references to the ICTY. I say that because that indicates the continuous nature of this process, how the Austrian procedure and the ICTY procedure are, in fact, bound up together. So, as I said at the outset of my submissions, you cannot put the OTP interviews in a little compartment and look at them in isolation. In our respectful submission you have to look at all that happened between 18th and 21st March, and using that evidence to decide has the thing gone wrong? Has this man had his rights breached? Was he misled? Did he get a fair explanation of what his rights were? Did he understand them? If he didn't, what we say is this: there has been a failure and the failure is such that under Rule 95 it undermines reliability, and in the second part of Rule 95 which deals with the admission being antithetical to and would seriously damage the integrity of the proceedings, the point is this: the standard that this Tribunal has set is set out in Rules 42 and 43, which relate to the questioning of suspects, and that is a standard -- if we fall below that, then that is one of the things which will affect the fairness of these proceedings. The whole purpose of those rules is to set a standard, and if some piece of evidence falls below that standard, which was a standard set with, no doubt, very careful thought by your Honours when coming to the conclusions as to what rules should be prevalent in this court, if it falls below that, then that's the test. It undercuts its reliability and it makes it antithetical to and would seriously damage, in our submission, the proceedings that you are holding. I think that's all I wish to say in reply to my learned friend. I am trying to be as brief as possible, but if there is any other matter I can assist your Honours on arising out of that, I shall be happy to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That's the reason I want that portion to be played.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In what details was his rights explained to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I do not dissent from the proposition that you should see it. MR. OLUJIC (in interpretation): With your permission, your Honours, before we view the videotape, I would only like to add something in support of what my colleague has explained in great detail, the symbiotic relationship of the police, on the one hand, and the investigators who arrived in Vienna on the other side. I would like to add on the basis of the transcript and the videotape it is clear that neither Mr. Abribat, the investigator of the Tribunal, or Mr. d'Hooge did not act in accordance with Rule 42 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, because they told my client that if he did not choose a lawyer that he would be assigned one by them, and they did not warn him that should he not select a lawyer, they -- they did not tell him that he did not have a right to defence, because that was his basic right, which comes out of the system, and this defence is a pre-condition that is absolutely based in the system. I would not like to repeat what my colleague has already said, but please, I plead that we watch very carefully when these two gentlemen are asking him this question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That's precisely the reason I want to see the tape, what was explained to him at the time he was being interviewed. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Can we now have the taped? (Videotape played).

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Today, 19th March 1996, at 3.30 in the afternoon we are in the premises of the Austrian Ministry of Justice in Vienna and are beginning the first interview of Mr. Zdravko Mucic, alias Pavo, who was arrested in front of his apartment on 18th March 1996 by the Austrian authorities. During the interview the following persons are present: Mr. Mucic in person, Ms Alexander Pal, the interpreter for the International Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, Mr. Bart d'Hooge, Peter Nicholson, and I myself, Regis Abribat. The three of us are members of the Prosecutor's Office of the International Tribunal in The Hague. Pursuant to the Statute of the Tribunal and the Rules of Procedure and Evidence I shall read Mr. Mucic his rights. He has the right to an attorney of his own choice, and if he cannot find one, an attorney will be assigned to him. He is entitled to interpreter's services free of charge. He has the right to remain silent and he is advised that everything he says will be recorded and can be used as evidence against him. I would also like to inform Mr. Mucic that this interview will be recorded on video and audio tapes and there will be a recording made of it and a copy of it will be given to him as soon as it is possible. Mr. Mucic, the first question is: do you agree to answer our questions without the presence of an attorney, as we have already discussed? Answer: Yes. Question: So, Mr. Mucic, I would like you to give us your personal data, your name, your last name, and the place and date of birth? Answer: My name is Zdravko Mucic".

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I think we can ask for it to be stopped now. Your Honours, I will point out that in addition to that on page 14 and, if your Honours want, we can have the -- during the lunch break we can find and queue up the portions, but it's reflected on page 14 of the English transcript. On March 20th at 9.30 hours Mr. Mucic was advised of his rights again and I can quote that. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I noticed one thing. I don't know whether any other person did. In the reading of his rights they still talked about "do you need a lawyer as we have discussed".

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: . That question was specifically asked to Mr. Abribat what that was in reference to. Mr. Abribat stated and the evidence supports that that was in reference to the brief conversation that they had had on the 18th. I will also point out, your Honour -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Because he has just read his rights to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That is correct. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Why did he have to refer to a discussion?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I believe Mr. Abribat indicated that he wanted to be very clear that there had been previous conversations, because there had been this very brief conversation on 18th, and Mr. Abribat wanted to ensure that this was made as of the record. Similarly later when during the break the attorney appointed to Mr. Mucic for extradition appeared when that came up later on, when the interview reviewed, another OTP investigator, this time Mr. d'Hooge, specifically made that part of the record. So I believe it was and I believe the testimony, the evidence is that it was an attempt to make sure that the record fairly and accurately reflected everything that had occurred, and because there had been this very brief conversation of the 18th, that that fact should be noted, that this was not the very first time that they had met each other. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: That other discussion is not on record.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the other discussion, which was not on interview, was not recorded. That is correct. It happened on the 18th. It lasted a few minutes. Mr. Regis Abribat and Mr. Gschwendt were present and testified about it. It was in order that they could introduce themselves to Mr. Mucic, so he knew who they were, and they explained that they, in fact, would like to interview him, and it would have to be in accordance with the Tribunal's rules of procedures. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you very much. I'm not expecting you to give any evidence at all. This is what somebody else should have told us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can find the portions of Mr. Regis Abribat's testimony, because he was specifically asked exactly about those words, and he gave his evidence about it, because I certainly agree I do not want to give any evidence. I will also note that on page 14 of the English transcript when the interview began on March 20th the same thing happens in that all the people are introduced, it's explained who they are, and Mr. Mucic is again advised of his rights. I can read that in its entirety, if it would assist the court. In particular after everyone is introduced Mr. Mucic is told: "He's entitled to have an attorney of his choice, and if he cannot afford one an attorney will be assigned to him. He's entitled to the services of an interpreter free of charge. In this case this is Ms. Pal, who is a certified interpreter at the International Tribunal. He has the right to remain silent and he's advised that a statement will be recorded and it will be used as evidence. We advise Mr. Mucic that this interview will be recorded and video and audio taped, that the recording will be transcribed and that Mr. Mucic will receive a copy of the transcript as soon as possible. Mr. Mucic, do you agree to answer our questions without the presence of an attorney? Answer: Yes." Then again on page 33 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just on the very first page, the portion which I witnessed, he was told that an attorney will be assigned to him, but he wasn't told it would be free of costs.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, he was told if he didn't have the possibility to get one himself, which I believe is another --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We can find it on the tape. One can be assigned to him, but not without any charge to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: It doesn't specifically use the words "free of charge" although that is used on March 20th, but, your Honour, we believe that the words "if he cannot get an attorney himself" encompasses both that he can't afford one and indeed if he doesn't know one. Your Honour, I believe, if anything, the slight difference of wording gives Mr. Mucic more rights rather than less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Not more rights, but he has a right to be told that no financial liability will fall on him if one is assigned to him?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I do understand that, your Honour. It is our submission when he is told if he doesn't have the possibility to get one himself, that encompasses that one will be assigned to him free of charge. To the extent there was any ambiguity about that whatsoever, and we don't believe there is, on 20th the words "free of charge" were specifically set out. So I would also point out that again after the lunch break on 20th on page 33 of the transcript Mr. Mucic is again informed of his rights, including his right to defence counsel of his choosing, and told if he does not have sufficient means to pay for defence counsel of his choosing, he has the right of defence counsel assigned to him and the rights are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just a minute. Here in the script of 19th March you use the words "free of charge" but I don't find it in the interview. Even in the portion which we have just read and which we have been shown.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. I am apparently not being clear. I'm agreeing on the 19th what was told to him was the words "free of charge".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But on your script you have provided to us this sentence occurs, that he is entitled to an interpreter's services free of charge.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am sorry. The term "free of charge" is not used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But it is in the script.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: For the interpreter. For the attorney it says: "If you do not" -- this is a translation but I believe it is in the effect of: "If you can't get one yourself". With respect to the attorney the words "free of charge" are not explicitly used. We believe that that is fairly encompassed and would have been understood to have been fairly encompassed within the motion that: "If you cannot get one yourself" which would include "if you cannot afford one". What I say is to the extent anyone would make an argument, which no one has, that the issue was one of money, we would point out that on subsequent occasions, for instance twice on March 20th, and I refer to page 14 of the transcript and page 33, the words -- he is specifically told that he can have an attorney "free of charge" and on page 33: "If he does not have sufficient means to pay for defence counsel of his own choosing". RULING The Prosecution seeks to tender in evidence the interviews of Mucic with the Austrian police and also with the investigators of the Office of the Prosecution into these proceedings. Mr. Greaves for Mucic objects and calls for the exclusion of both interviews. In his submission before the Trial Chamber Mr. Greaves pointed out that the rights of a suspect under Austrian law are an offence against provisions of Rules 42 of Rules of Procedure and Evidence. He went on to point out that there was no unfettered right to counsel and the right of silence is qualified. The provision encouraging the suspect to confess is very similar to an inducement to do so to secure mitigation of punishment. Learned counsel referred to the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984, Section 76, which governs cases of confession in England. It was argued, in fact, that the interviewee admitted being tired and the interview of the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor with Mucic continued for more than five and a half hours with interviews alternating, as there was among two or three interviews indicated that Mucic himself must have been tired in the process and the statements made thereby inadmissible. The cross-culture involved in the exercise might have introduced confusion in the mind of Mucic. The interviews involved too distant and somewhat contradictory rights in the legal systems. Mr. Abribat admitted to have explained the suspect's rights in a few minutes. It was unnecessary to have conducted the interview in Austria at the time when extradition proceedings had already begun. It was therefore more convenient to have done so at the Hague, to where in any event Mucic was being extradited. The Prosecution have not proved the waiver. There is the outstanding question of what was discussed with Mr. Abribat. The burden of proof rests on the Prosecution. It is beyond reasonable doubt. The sum total is that the statements sought to be tendered must be reliable, which are the principles of the Tadic Decision and our rules on reliability. The three interviews should be considered together for the purposes of reliability and admissibility. Ms McHenry for the Prosecution submits that the burden of proof of voluntariness is not in our rules proved beyond reasonable doubt. The standard of proof differs from country to country. Counsel does not think that rules of Austrian police relating to warning of suspects is either improper or in violation of recognised human rights provisions. It was argued that the tiredness of the suspect was not a factor throughout the interview, and indeed Mucic never indicated he was tired or exhausted. He was throughout the interview in control of himself and answers to questions. Learned counsel submitted that the two interviews were separate and conducted by different persons for different purposes and at different times. They should be separate for the purpose of determining the admissibility of the statements resulting from the interviews. Counsel referred to the evidence of Mr. Gschwendt and Abribat who, it was argued, have cleared the doubts about the question of a previous conversation between Mucic and Abribat. There is not evidence of the 20 minutes gap after the investigating judge had concluded than is on the record. There is no interview. Abribat merely introduced the investigating team. In all the circumstances the Office of the Prosecution has behaved properly and in conformity with the law. After considering all the arguments, the Trial Chamber states as follows. The Trial Chamber is governed by its Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Accordingly any evidence to be admissible in proceedings before it must satisfy the law as provided in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The Tribunal is established for the trial of criminal offences of the most serious kind. Nothing less than most exacting standard of proof is required. It is universally accepted that the burden of proof rests entirely on the Prosecution and this it must establish beyond reasonable doubt. This is the standard of proof required in this Trial Chamber. The issue before the Trial Chamber is the admissibility of the statements made by the accused as suspects before the Austrian police and before the Office of the Prosecution. Learned counsel has described them as a single exercise and to be rejected because of the violations of the rules of the Tribunal governing interrogation of suspects. The Prosecutor submits the two interviews are separable and could be separated for the purposes of considering the reliability and admissibility of the statements. It is not disputable that the two interviews are separate both in fact and in law. The Austrian interview is governed by Austrian law, whereas the interview by the Office of the Prosecutor is governed by our Rules. There is no doubt the Austrian rules governing is clearly different and contradictory to our own Rules. The test of having counsel at interview, right to silence, essentially Rule 42, are not essential in the Austrian provisions. The suggestion of a suspect confessing is absent in our Rule 42. Accordingly that Austrian law is subject to the test of Rule 42 is likely to fail. On the other hand, there is very little other than the consideration of the two interviews because of the continuous existence that will affect the OTP interview. Considering them together, the witness would have been exposed to an inordinate length of examination which is likely to affect his concentration and ability to react to questioning. This is, however, a question of fact, but the Trial Chamber considers his fitness, his experience and surrounding circumstances that he was not affected by the length of interview. There is nothing to show that he was affected even by the cross-culture. The series of new warnings as to his rights by the OTP investigators were sufficient to erase any impressions from any inducement to confess held out him by the Austrian police investigators. There is sufficient evidence that the suspect waived his right to counsel. The Trial Chamber is satisfied that the interview of the Austrian police does not satisfy Rule 42. It is, therefore, not reliable and cannot be admitted into evidence. The interview conducted by the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor comply with the provisions of Rule 42. It is reliable and admissible. The interview is admissible. The weight to be attached and the probative value will be determined by considering all the other circumstances in these proceedings. This is our Ruling. Ms. McHenry, do you have any other thing to say, because we have a joint application here?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours will probably recall that at the end of the testimony of Mr. d'Hooge the Prosecution offered the statement of Mr. Landzo. At that point I rose and asked that it be deferred until I'd had an opportunity to develop an objection by way of a cross-examination that I intended to conduct. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I think you can, because I was expecting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I do want to reiterate the argument that I made to your Honours in connection with a motion I filed earlier in this case for leave to file a motion, and at that point you'll recall that I argued about the cultural and legal differences between the lawyer that was representing Mr. Landzo at the time the statement was made and his lack of understanding of the common law rules that were being applied to that. Although I haven't got an order from the court on that issue yet, it was pretty clear from the bench what your attitude was about that argument, but I do want to just by reference include that as part of my argument today. The second part, on page 3 of the English version of the Landzo interview Mr. d'Hooge, and that is right at the very beginning, makes the following statement: "I have asked the interpreter not to interpret every single word, essentially when we are speaking about background matters". You will also recall that I cross-examined him about that. Now I learned, having come late into this case, and I was making an argument recently, and I learned it is this Chamber's position that the rules are applied rather strictly -- the rules of this Chamber are applied rather strictly and I was, therefore, not permitted to file a motion to raise further objections to this statement, and I think that the rules probably should be applied rather strictly, and if they are applied rather strictly: “I have asked the interpreter not to interpret every single word, especially when we are speaking about background matters" seems to me to be in complete and total violation of a combination of Rules 42 and 43. Now, this is capable, I believe, of being solved, but it hasn't been solved at this point. It may be that the Prosecution has not called all the witnesses necessary to lay the foundation, and let me see if I can explain this. It's a little bit difficult. If the interpreter, and I am anticipating Ms McHenry's argument to some extent, is told not to interpret every single word, the mere existence of a contemporaneous Serbo-Croatian transcript does not solve the problem, because the question is not whether there was a contemporaneous Serbo-Croatian transcript, but whether the question asked by Mr. d'Hooge in English was translated into Serbo-Croatian in the same terms so that the question that Mr. d'Hooge was asking in English was understood by Mr. Landzo the way it was interpreted in Serbo-Croatian, so that the answer that he gave when it was interpreted back into English was related to the question that was originally asked in English. That's where I think the deficiency is. There's no way -- Mr. d'Hooge admitted on cross-examination that he does not understand Serbo-Croatian so he has no ability to tell us and had no ability to tell us what it was that the interpreter may have left out of the translations at his direction to not interpret every single word, especially background matters. That is such an imprecise instruction. The "don't interpret every single word, especially when we're speaking about background matters", that there's no way to know how the interpreter may have interpreted what he told the interpreter to do. It may have been taken broadly, and therefore significant material left out of the questions that were asked; it may have been taken very narrowly and virtually nothing left out; it may have been ignored by the interpreter and there may have been a complete interpretation, but the only way that we can know that is if the interpreter is here on the witness stand. If the interpreter were to come here and say: "I have reviewed the Serbo-Croatian tape and compared it with the translations I made into English, and I, in fact, ignored Mr. d'Hooge and interpreted everything. Every question that was asked was completely interpreted and every answer that was given was completely interpreted", then I think I would not be able to make an objection, because I think it would have been taken in accordance with Rules 42 and 43. So I'm not suggesting that there is a permanent defect here. I'm suggesting that there is a temporary defect that maybe is capable of being solved, but the only way we can know is if the Prosecution brings that interpreter here, and it would take maybe five minutes. "Question: Have you reviewed it? Answer: Yes, I have. Question: Was anything left out? Answer: No, it wasn't". Then we could all be satisfied that it was conducted in accordance with the rules. I think until that happens we can't, because once there is that instruction given: "Do not interpret every single word", there is a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHITE
utterances.text: Did you ask Mr. d'Hooge what he regarded as background matters, because it limited that she should not interpret word by word by referring to background matters? What did he say he regarded background matters to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't recall that he gave an answer in that, your Honour, because -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Because that is limiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No. If he said: "Don't do ..." -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Even if you do not, whoever interprets word for word in every language? It is not done that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I am not suggesting it has to be done that way. We have limited time so don't interpret every single word, especially when speaking about background", unless we can be certain that Mr. Landzo understood in his language the questions that Mr. d'Hooge was asking in English, then we can't be certain that the answers to those questions are related to the English question. That's where the problem is. It's not a question where we could challenge every interpretation in this court and have to bring every interpreter that ever did an interpretation here to testify. It's when it is said to an interpreter: "Don't do it the regular way but do it this way this time because we are in a hurry that there is a question".

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, like Mr. Ackerman, I filed a motion under Rule 73C and have not received a ruling. I'm not going to argue with the prospective ruling of the court, and I've got a pretty good idea what it is, but just to guarantee that any kind of error, if there is any, is preserved, I think I need to make a couple of minutes of argument and objection to the admission of Mr. Delic's statement. As the court will recall, he actually had counsel sitting next to him when he gave both of the recorded statements, and no one is suggesting that the rules -- that Rule 42 and 43 were not complied with. However, the right to counsel, something that's guaranteed by our Statute, something that's guaranteed by the European convention of human rights, I found it in Article 8 of the inter-American Convention of Human Rights, I would suggest it is more than just having a lawyer, someone licensed to practice law some place. It includes the right to have a lawyer who is familiar with the law that's being applied. Judge Jan said something this morning that frankly I didn't know about the law in Pakistan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: A statement made by an accused before the police is inadmissible in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is, as I understand it, the same thing as the law in Yugoslavia. Now you and I come from the same legal tradition. Basically we speak -- and Judge Karibi-White also -- all three of us speak the same legal language with twists and turns to it, obviously with our national differences, and I would submit to you if I suddenly found myself in Pakistan representing someone who was suspected of an offence and being questioned by the police, my knee jerk reaction would be: "You don't talk", because the law in America is very, very different from the law in Pakistan. On the other hand, a very fine lawyer from Pakistan dropped into Houston, Texas, representing a Pakistani, might very well say: "Go ahead and talk to officer so-and-so, because it can't be used against you". Then the question becomes: is that a knowing waiver of his right to silence when it's based on that kind of advice? I'm suggesting that a court could find that that waiver was not a knowing waiver and therefore not a voluntary waiver. I would also suggest that when you say voluntary as it's used in the rules, it means something other than: "Okay, I'll talk if you loosen the thumb screws". It has to be a knowing waiver. You have to know what you're doing. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Wouldn't we prefer a mistaken waiver?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: A mistaken waiver or -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Not that he didn't know he was waiving but if he knew better, he would not have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that's a good way of doing it. The knowing would be what we would say in the United States, that you don't understand the consequences of your waiver. Again that would be a mistaken waiver. I think that, given Mr. Delic's written statement to the court, which is attached to my Rule 73 motion, and the status of the law in Yugoslavia, the kind of advice one would be given by someone who is familiar with that system and not familiar with the system used in the Tribunal, which is frankly very familiar to me, because it's right out of my Supreme Court rules, and on each side of me I've got a very good friend who is a Yugoslav lawyer and I think they are both fine lawyers and I think both of them would stand up here and tell you at the time they talked to their clients and their clients talked to the investigators from the Tribunal, they were under the misapprehension that the law would be applied as it would be in Yugoslavia or in Pakistan. Their advice to their client was based upon that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I am not doubting the competence of counsel which Delalic had at the time, but I'm sure any lawyer would study the rules of the Tribunal before giving any advice to his client.
