I am not doubting the competence of counsel. This is done by senior counsel. They read the rules and the rules clearly state: "This evidence will be used against you".

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am not disagreeing with you at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Because you are not giving advice to a client if you don't know the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: What I am suggesting is I am not focusing on the attorneys at this point. I am suggesting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I think your argument basically is that the counsel was not aware of the law here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I am suggesting that the advice and everything that went into the advice and also how the client understood the advice should be viewed along the lines of the law that people are familiar with. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Occasionally we have to think about it but, you know, would you regard mistake of law as an excuse in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: As a defence, your Honour? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: For this purpose, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: For this purpose I haven't thought it through. I can tell you what my view would be on mistake of law as an absolute defence to a crime, which would be that if it's a reasonable mistake of law that -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Now you have added the other word "reasonable".

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sitting next to a law Professor who has probably been known during recitation to say: "Let's change the facts". The rule that I'm used to on mistake of law is this, your Honour, that if it's a reasonable mistake of law, that is it's based on some kind of a -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: That is if the knowledge of the law is a factor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, if it's based on some kind of a court decision or a Statute or something like that, where I might think I have the right to do this act, to take this computer home with me, and it turns out that I don't, then I'm not guilty of the crime because I have relied upon an order from the Trial Chamber that I could take this computer home with me, even though the Registrar would complain about it a little later. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: It would not be a mistake if you say you have an order. You might have an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I think when we are talking about the waiver of a right you have to look into whether that waiver -- again in my parlance -- is a knowing waiver, that you know what it's doing so that the -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I agree. A person does not waive something unless he knew about that. That's the sense of that thing. That's only when you can waive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And the consequences of waiver. I am suggesting as it applied to Mr. Delic and probably Mr. Delalic, although I am sure not going to make an argument for them because they can make their own arguments, they are fine lawyers, I am suggesting that he might not have known -- that he did not know the consequences of the waiver. No one is accusing the Office of the Prosecutor of doing anything wrong, and I don't want anyone to think that I am. What I'm just suggesting is that he was dropped and his lawyer was dropped into a situation involving a legal system that is again something that -- the first time I read these rules, they read like my federal rules of criminal procedure to a great extent, and I'm very used to the procedural rules at least in general here, but when you get someone from a country that has a completely different legal system, a lawyer and a client who are used to dealing with completely different legal systems, that you get into the knowingness of that, and that's my suggestion, and that's my objection to the admissibility. Again I've got a real good idea what the Trial Chamber is going to Rule on my Rule 73 motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Don't anticipate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: If per chance -- if I'm wrong, I'm very happy and I appreciate it. If I'm right, I wouldn't want the Trial Chamber to think that I'm arguing after a decision is made. Once a decision is made, it's made and we all live with it. I thank the Trial Chamber for its time. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you very much. It's a lot of interesting and very beautiful arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I don't know whether you would welcome some assistance on the slightly different position of ignorance of the law in English law, which is different from that which Mr. Moran knows. Ignorance of the law in English law is no defence, although it can afford significant mitigation, which I think is a slightly different position from that which my learned friend has in his jurisdiction. I suspect it may be similar in your Honour's jurisdiction and Judge Jan. I see Judge Odio Benito says the same. I hope that's helpful.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will just very briefly respond. I will note also that I thought there had been an oral decision made also about the Rule 73, but I may well be wrong. In any event, the Prosecution believes that it is beyond question that the accused understood his rights and the consequences from waiving those rights. We believe any contrary claim is frankly incredible. We would also note that we don't believe that the Defence should be allowed to make sort of vague allegations about what may or may not have been advised without waiving the attorney/client privileges so we can tell, but in any event what is clear and beyond dispute is that the accused was told in his own language of his rights, which include that he had the right to remain silent, but anything he said would be recorded and could be used in evidence. I don't believe that there can be any misunderstanding of this very clear and non-complicated provision. The Defence counsel or his attorney -- the accused himself had a chance to ask questions if he was confused, and he did not. We would also note, although we think it's unnecessary, because we believe the clear language of the rules controls and makes it clear that the accused who is mentally competent did understand exactly what he was doing, that in June of 1996, prior to the first interview of Mr. Delic, the Defence of Mr. Delalic had filed a motion seeking to exclude Mr. Delalic's prior statement making it very clear that there was already law in this court that statements would be used against you, and indeed in the beginning of December, prior to Mr. Delic's second interview, the Prosecution had, in fact, sent the Defence, including the Defence of Mr. Delic, a letter in which we formally stated that we would use the statements of all accused as evidence against them, or that it was our intention to do so. So we do not believe that there can be any claim that the accused did not understand exactly what he was doing. The rules were fully complied with. There was a presumption that the statements are admissible and we believe all the facts and circumstances also support the admission of the statements. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I've made my point and I think that the Trial Chamber understands my point. If there's any questions, I will be happy to try to answer them as best I can. If there aren't any, I'm going to sit down. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Thank you very much. Thank you very much. I think instead of wasting your time and asking you to be concerned about other witnesses, I agree we will admit the statements, but, as I said in the last ruling, all these statements will be subject to other circumstances affecting the weight to be attached to what these admissions are, so that they are not by being admitted described as the truth of what is being put forward. We will still consider whether these really satisfy the rules themselves. They are admitting them for the purposes of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I want to thank the Trial Chamber for the consideration and I also just want to point out that it has been -- the way this Trial Chamber has ruled on several other things is something that I think a lot of courts ought to consider doing. You are always willing to take a second look at the admissibility of evidence that has been previously admitted. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: We watch everyone. This is not the last word. This is what I keep saying. It is not the last word. Merely because a statement is admitted does not mean it has proved what it is being admitted for.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I frankly wish the courts in my jurisdiction would adopt the more enlightened rule that this Trial Chamber has where we can always take a second look at the admissibility of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You are drawing the distinction between the admissibility and the probative value. The probative value has to be determined after taking into consideration all the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That's true. Something inadmissible has to probative value because it is not here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It's not before us. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: It has to be weighed against all the other factors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Like I say, this Trial Chamber seems to be taking a very enlightened view on both of those subjects. I would like to see more of it when I get home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You need to be congratulated because you anticipated correctly our decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I missed it, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You ought to be congratulated for correctly anticipating our decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I got trained in law school. That's what we are trained to do, guess what judges will do. I thought I had a pretty good guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The real trick is guessing what juries do. That is a fine art. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I suppose that's all for today.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: We have a witness, if your Honours want us to call the next fact witness. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Let's have the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: The Prosecution calls Mr. Dordic. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Please swear the witness. Mr. Novica Dordic (sworn) Examined by Ms McHenry

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, may I ask you to state your full name, please? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I hope the interpretation is getting through to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't hear the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you hear me now, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, would you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Novica Dordic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, am I correct that you have not requested any protective measures connected with your testimony here today, in other words you are happy for your name to be known?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'm going to ask that when you answer my questions you speak very slowly, and I will probably remind you of that during your testimony, so I'll just warn you now. How old are you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am 28.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far did you go in school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have secondary education.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your ethnic background, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the beginning of 1992 where were you living?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the village of Zukici near Konjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you employed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was working in the railway transportation service of Sarajevo, the unit in Bradina. I was working in the railway transportation service of Sarajevo in the unit at Bradina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did there come a time when you left Zukici, as it was no longer your residence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked in Bradina and I went to work regularly until there was transportation, until it was working. I left Zukici somewhere around 24th April because it was not safe to stay there any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because -- I went to Bradina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In May of 1992 was there any military action in Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Bradina military operations were -- let me tell you. Problems had already started in Sarajevo and Mostar. I don't know myself what was happening, some kind of a war. There was fighting, I don't know for what reasons, and almost all the ethnic groups -- all people joined up with their ethnic group. Just as I went to Bradina, so in Podrazic, in Konjic, the Muslim and Croat forces and Serb forces were separating one from another. There was no inter-ethnic communication as before. People didn't contact amongst each other inter-ethnically. They were separating.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I am going to object to this as non-responsive. The question was, was there military action in Bradina in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I think the witness is leading up to the answer. As a result of what you have just described, sir, are you aware of whether or not there was any military action, meaning fighting, or attacks, or defences, in Bradina in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't exactly know the date, but the tunnel was blown up just below Bradina, it is a tunnel on the highway, and I think that with the blowing up of that tunnel tensions in the whole municipality were heightened, and I personally saw that tunnel. I was still in Zukici at the time. I was staying with a relative near the highway -- near the tunnel, maybe 250 or 300 metres from the tunnel, and in the evening some vehicles came up, because at that time there was no movement of vehicles, especially not at all, and some vehicles came. It was night-time. They entered the tunnel. We were looking out to see what was happening, because there were four or five vehicles moving, and they reached the tunnel. They switched off their lights. We watched them. We could actually see only the lights. At some point in time two or three vehicles came back. After that something terrible happened. A glimmering light appeared and a terrible explosion was heard, probably coming from one of the vehicles on the highway just below us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, at some point after the tunnel was blown up was there any additional military action in Bradina itself, and I mean --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Bradina people were in a panic after that. People who had transistor radios, as there was no electricity, were listening to Konjic radio, which blamed us for mining the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to have to object as non-responsive. The question was: "Was there any military action in May" and he is going on to another speech. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, at this point it's not necessary for you to describe the background. Can you just tell me whether or not there came a time when for various reasons there was actually military action, meaning that the village was attacked or forces from within or without engaged in any kind of fighting or shelling or shooting?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I'm going to say we have no objection to Ms McHenry leading the witness on that question. Thank you. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Actually limit your answer to Bradina. Is that what you want him to do? You should not go --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, sir. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Don't make it wider. Stop at Bradina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Because that will expand the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour, for the warning. Sir, just with respect to Bradina itself, was there a time when there was some sort of fighting or shooting or shelling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I just wanted to provide more detail, but what happened was there was fighting on the hill of Velika on 13th May, if I remember the date correctly. It's a hill above Bradina. There was some shooting there. Who was firing at whom I don't know. I only know that we heard reports that we had been attacked, that we had to defend ourselves, that whoever had any weapons should go there, and this went on for about two days and then it calmed down until 25th May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just very briefly, sir, what happened on 25th May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 25th May I don't know exactly, somewhere in the afternoon, fighting resumed on that same hill and then shells started falling on Bradina, and this went on all of that afternoon until late at night, and it continued the next day. I was in a wood near the highway. No one was firing at me, nor were there any operations there. Then we returned to Bradina to see what was happening. This was the second day when most of Bradina was on fire. The houses in Bradina were mostly hit by shells.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time of these events, sir, were you armed and, if so, with what kind of weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was armed with an automatic rifle of Yugoslav make.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you get your weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I got it through a friend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to the attack had you participated in any armed defence of Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, except after May 13th watch duty was organised along the surrounding hills.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you participate in the watch duty and, if so, were you armed at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I participated in these duties and I was armed, because it is normal to be armed if you're on a hilltop in the woods, at night especially.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could, sir, just briefly describe what you did when the attack on Bradina started and you went to the woods and came back leading up to the point of describing whether or not at some point you were captured or arrested, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me tell you when we got to Bradina there were three of us in my group. There was chaos in Bradina. There was a white flag flying in the centre. They said there were a lot of casualties but we had no idea what was actually happening. We reached a cafe which had a very large cellar and mostly women and children were housed there. It was chaotic. There was crying and weeping. They told us that we had to decide what we were going to do, either to flee or to give ourselves up. So we fled. We fled towards the other part of Bradina, which is removed from the centre, and it's closer to the mountains, and we found more 20 or so people there, who were also ready to flee. They didn't dare wait for the Muslim and Croat forces to enter Bradina. So we mostly climbed across the mountains the next four or five days. We decided to head towards Kalinovik, because there was fighting in Hadici and Sarajevo already and we didn't know what would happen to us there. There was shooting at us from the surrounding hills. We don't know who was firing. We had three or four lightly wounded people and we later learned the village was called Ljuta where we arrived and there was very intensive shooting from the surrounding hills and then we dispersed. One of us went down a path. His name was Zaro Mrkajic. I later learned that he had gone to the village. He later called on us to surrender. He said that those people didn't do anything wrong, that they just wanted to collect our weapons and that they would transfer us to Kalinovik. So we decided to that path and these people really did treat us decently. Nobody beat us, nor did they do anything bad to us. They just took our weapons and it was already dark so that they couldn't transfer us to Kalinovik that same night, but by the next day that they would take us there and there would be no problems. We agreed to that. Then they took us to a schoolhouse in the village. I think it was a school, a building anyway. They put us up there and they told us to dry up, because we were all wet, tired and hungry. Shortly afterwards a man entered with an automatic rifle and he started shooting into the ceiling of this premise that we were in. He ordered us to lie down. Then some other men came in, not those from before. They started beating us with various objects, rifles, anything they could get hold of. They called us Cetniks. They said that this man who had entered first, that his brother-in-law had been killed or something like that, and they continued beating us until late that night. That moment I saw two young men with HOS insignia on their uniform sleeves and very short hair. This went on, this beating, this heavy beating. Then they found pieces of wire. I didn't see handcuffs. They tied our hands with this wire and I think it must have been just before dawn, about 3 o'clock, they took us somewhere from this school, and we got up as far as we could, because we were all beaten up. Each one of us had his own guard. The people in the village had woken up. They beat us with various objects. As we passed by in a column, they insulted us. We didn't know why. Then we had to go on through a wood, across some hills. I don't exactly know where we were. We went on until we reached a path where two small trucks were waiting. The beatings continued. They climbed us into these two small trucks and under protection of guards they took us somewhere. At that moment at least I wasn't aware where I was. They unloaded us in a village I later learned. I remember there was a prefabricated building there, a school or something like that, and I heard people talking and mentioning the village of Sabici, so it was probably the village of Sabici. We spent maybe around one hour in that school. They continued to beat us, to mistreat us, to swear at us. Then they loaded us on to a bigger truck. I don't exactly know the make. Then again under the escort of five or six young men -- I must say they were very young, 16, 17, 18 on the outside -- they took us away. Again I heard from the conversation the guards were having that we were crossing Mount Igman. All that time these young boys were beating us, hitting us with various objects, which they were carrying in addition to the rifles that they normally had. They were kicking us with boots, hitting us and climbing on our shoulders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did they bring you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took us later -- not I but other people realised it was the Famos Hotel on Mount Igman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go after you were at the Famos Hotel? Did you stay there or were you brought somewhere else after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the Famos Hotel they took us out in front of the hotel and we headed for the trucks. There were about 100-150 people there, mostly women and elderly, and the other side there was the army, the military, and they kept hitting us, cursing at us, saying that we were Cetniks, and calling us by all kinds of names, up to this truck. We climbed on it and the same guards with there, and suddenly the truck veered from the asphalt road. It must have come across a hole in the road. I heard shooting above my head. A guard that was sitting on the side of the truck behind me was shooting and I saw a man who was sitting leaning on my knee, that his sweater was torn in the area of the heart. This was a relative of mine called Dragan Vujicic who died on the spot from the bullets fired from that rifle. Three or four other people were wounded on that occasion. One of them lost an eye. I thought he was dead. No one did anything except putting on a bandage, so that they couldn't look at him because it was a terrible sight. Then from the mutual conversation I heard that they were taking us to Konjic. They mistreated us all the time. They beat us. They took out SDA badges and HDZ badges from their pockets, forcing us to kiss them. Then they even got a dead boar and through it into the truck, saying it was our symbol and forcing us to kiss it. Then we were taken in front of the SUP building in Konjic. By that time I could hardly see from the beatings. My eyes were almost closed. I could hardly discern anything. Anyway, we were not allowed to look left or right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Were you brought anywhere after you were brought to the SUP building in Konjic? Were you then brought anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we weren't taken into the building of SUP but only the courtyard of the SUP building and then the leaders of the SUP at the time came out. Jasmin Guska, Sefic Niksic, Diksa and Miro Stenek, all of them were there. I heard them insulting Rajko Dordic, who was a colleague of theirs, why he was with us. He was the worst. He was a duke, a "vujvujda". Then some boys, young men beat us in front of there. Then they took us out of town. I didn't dare lift up my head, but at one point I saw that we were in front of the Konjic motel on the way out of the town, and I saw on the terrace of the motel that there were many soldiers. They were cursing, firing into the air and celebrating the fact that they had captured us, and then we went on. Very soon after that we found ourselves in a building which I did not know from before. It was my first time to be there. Anyway my freedom of movement was limited. I couldn't look around. We were lined up against a wall, facing the wall, so that I couldn't see anything. I could just feel the blows.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object as non-responsive. In this story I've lost where we go now. Can we just kind of figure out where he is located at this point?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, at this point were you inside a building or just inside a place?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am sorry, are we still in Konjic or are we --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am going to get there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, at the time you have just described when you were placed against a wall, were you inside a building or outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were in a kind of compound. We had passed through the gate. At the time I didn't know that it was the Celebici camp and the barracks of the former Yugoslav people's army. We were lined up, we were beaten and then I saw the body of Dragan Vujicic that was thrown into the container.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I object as non-responsive. She just asked what building he was in and where it was located. Could we keep it to question and answer form, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me just ask you: the compound you were in, am I correct that you learned that it was called the Celebici and it was the former barracks of the Yugoslav Army? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I knew that we must have been near Celebici, because the drive lasted about ten minutes. I was born in Konjic, so I'm familiar with the municipality of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us -- so approximately what was the date that you were actually brought to Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was 30th or 31st May 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long overall did you remain in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From that time until -- I don't know the exact date but I think it was 20 days before the camp was closed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: October, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: October of 1992, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About how many persons were brought to Celebici at the same time as you were, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 22, 23, maybe less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there already other prisoners in Celebici when your group arrived, or were you the first prisoners to go to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time I didn't know that it was a camp even nor whether there were any prisoners inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time, though, that you learned whether or not you were the first group of prisoners or whether or not there were already prisoners there before your group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A long time after that I learned that before me, quite a long time before me, there were prisoners there, but I learned that later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, can you please briefly describe what happened when you first arrived at the camp? I believe you started to say you were placed against the wall. Can you just briefly describe what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was just starting to describe that. As I was saying, we were lined up against a wall. We were already exhausted. Our hands were tied. They would take away one or two from this column that I was in. I didn't know where I was. I didn't dare turn around, but as this body was very close to me, I saw it being taken away in a container. I'm saying this to show how brutal it was, how they treated this corpse. Then they came for me, two heavily built men in uniform much bigger than I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Before you get to that, the body that you saw, I believe you said it was Dragan Vujicic. Was he the person who had been killed on the truck, just so that everyone can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I think let's have a break now and we will return at 4.30. (4.00 pm) (Short break) (4.30pm). JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Let's have the witness. Ms McHenry, I hope you will try and get your witness restrained. He wants to say everything he has in mind. Let's get on with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. He has a lot of information. I think once we are at Celebici it will be directed. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I don't think he wants to be guided. Try and let him know that we have a time limit for everything. (Witness re-enters court) JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Remind him he is on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I should like to remind you that you are still testifying under oath.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, I believe you had indicated that after you were on the wall and people were being beaten two men came up to you. Can you just tell us what happened when these two men came up to you? What happened next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When these two heavy men came up to me they caught me by my hands that were tied behind my back and my shoulders, and they took me to a building that was behind my back at the time. They took me through a corridor and then from one of the rooms a young man ran out. He hit me two or three times, mostly with his leg. He kicked me in the chest. After that they took me into an office, where Miro Stenek was seated. These were people who used to be working in SUP, and Sefik Niksic. There was a woman there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am going to object. The question was when the two men came up behind you at the wall, what did they do to you? Now he has gone into another story. The objection is non-responsive.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I think this is entirely responsive. I asked him what happened next. He is telling me. Certainly this is the information I wanted that I believe is relevant and the witness should hear. I believe it is responsive to what happened next and is directly relevant to these proceedings. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: He is responding to what happened after the two men. It is a continuation of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes. What happened next is a vague question, your Honour, and it leaves the door -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: That is what he understood.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: -- too wide for this examination. If we could just narrow the scope of the questions, I believe he would be able to respond more accurately. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Since he is responding with directly relevant testimony, sir, if you could just continue with what happened when you were -- when there were these two men and the woman in the room what happened next. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: What happened to him next.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes. What happened, sir, after you were brought into this room? What happened to you after you were brought into the room with the people you described in it? Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They sat me down in a chair facing the two of them and they said -- they asked me whether I knew why I was there. I said: "No". They said that I should make a statement about everything that had happened in Bradina and around it and how I had been brought to that building, that compound. At that moment I was not aware where I was. They started asking me questions whether I had been armed, what arms I had, where I was when we were attacking. They were saying that we were attacking instead of us having been attacked. All that we said at that hearing, all the questions, were mostly put by Sefik Niksic, and, as I was saying, they asked about things that I didn't know about, nor did I know that there were so many casualties in Bradina, that there were many dead. They asked me whether I knew what we had done. I was astonished. I didn't know what they meant. What had we done to make us responsible for all this? What weapons I had; who had given me those weapons. All this was taken down. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Do you understand him?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. He is talking about his interrogation. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: "Us" and "we" he is talking about. Do you understand who all those people are?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I believe I do. Let me clarify it. Sir, when you talk about "us", are you talking about the people who were in Bradina? When they were asking you about what happened in Bradina, when you say: "They were asking about why we did this", are you referring to you and the other people in Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were thinking of the people in Bradina. What they had done they were accusing us of doing it. They said that we were to blame for what had happened in Bradina. It was from them that I had learned that such a major event had taken place in Bradina and that there were many dead, but I knew nothing about that at the time. I had been in Bradina, I had fled Bradina and I didn't know what had happened. I only know about Dragan Vujicic's death, who died at my feet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, after they asked you any questions -- after they asked you the questions that you have just told us about, did they ask you to sign anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They asked me to sign, to sign this whole statement that I had made, and they put the paper and a pencil before me. I got up, but my hands were still tied, and then Niksic was pointing to the paper and asking me to sign and I wondered how I could sign. That was the first time for me in my life to be forced to do so, to be beaten, to be tied up and I tried to sign with my hands tied and then one of these men who had brought me to that room hit me. He forced me into the chair again. Niksic told them to untie my hands and I signed something, a statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to read what you signed or did anyone read it to you before you signed it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were your hands tied with, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some kind of wire that was 3-4 mms thick.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, the room that you were interrogated in, do you know what direction it faced? Did it face the medical building or did it face the outside of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was facing the building which was later the medical building. I learned later that Dr. Relja and Dr. Petko were there and it was a kind of dispensary. So from that office I could see that building of the dispensary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After your interrogation, sir, what happened next? Were you brought somewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They tied me up again and they took me out back against the wall, together with the other people who had been interrogated and who had been questioned like me, so we were lined up against the wall again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then what happened next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We waited there for some time. I think there were two more people that had not been interrogated that had to be questioned after me, and when they finished they ordered us to go along a path. Later I learned that we were heading for building Number 9, where I was incarcerated all the time. Then they brought us in front of the tunnel. They lined us up and then a man appeared. I learned later that he was Hazim Delic. I think he was limping. They opened this building Number 9 and they took out from there, I don't know the exact number, but there were certainly 70-80 people. These people were mostly from Bradina, mostly elderly people, and they lined us up opposite us (sic). Then Hazim ordered them to face us and we were at a distance of 3-4 metres between us, and then he started telling them that this group which I was in was to blame for everything that had happened in Bradina. He called us Cetnik gang, and then he took those people away somewhere, and we were imprisoned in the premises where they had been. This cell was an ordinary tunnel about 1.40 metres wide, and there was an inclination going downwards. It was about 30-odd metres long. On the walls we could see traces of blood and remnants of clothing from the people who had been incarcerated there before us. The doors were closed on us and nobody interfered with us after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask that you look in front of you, and maybe the clerk could please help him with the pointer, and ask you if you recognise that large model in front of you and, if so, you can point out the areas that you have mentioned, including where you were taken for interrogation, the wall you were placed against, and then building Number 9 that you have referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first we were brought here in front of -- at first we were lined up in front of this building marked with the letter C and from there we were led into this building. Probably this first or second window is the window of the office of the one of these two windows. Then from there we were lined up again in front and then led along this path to this wall here, which I can't see from here. Then we were lined up somewhere here where we had just brought in, and those people came out of this building here I think. The door was opened where I'm showing and that is where those 80-odd people came out from, and they were lined up along this canal and we were standing here. After what I have already said, they were taken away in that direction and we were placed inside this building. (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, as long as you are using the model now just in an effort to save time can you tell us any other areas -- just show us any other areas of the model that you came to be familiar with at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For this time that I have been talking about I knew nothing else than I have told you, but later on I learned about the other buildings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Why don't you just now tell us about the other buildings that you became familiar with and the other areas, and then I believe it may just help later on when you are explaining -- JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Why do you want it now? There is everything relevant you can talk about.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, if you just sit down, I will wait until we get to those parts. Can you describe what the conditions were like in Tunnel 9 -- I'm sorry -- in building 9, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I have already said, there was a metal door in the front and it goes from one end of the building to the other. The door had two parts. There was about a 10 per cent decline, and after maybe some 20 metres it straightens out at the end, so that when you just enter the building it doesn't go straight forward but it has a turning to the left. This flat area is only about 3 or 4 metres and then at the bottom of this building was a large metal gate with a ventilator, and on the ceiling I think there were two neon lights. There are no other openings except an opening of about 50 by 40 on both sides of the door. Rough concrete was on the floor and that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe where you slept, where you went to the bathroom, just the living conditions that you had while you were in the building Number 9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first while we were not so numerous and there was just my group there was sufficient space for us at least to be able to sit down decently. We could lean against the wall. But with time I think at one point there were 45 of us there. They were transferred to this building. I don't know where they came from, so that it was very cramped. There was very little space for 45 people. We had to leave some space next to the door, about 2 metres, because that was the order from the prison authorities, and we had to manage with the rest of the space. We would lie cross ways on the slope so we were not lying down in the direction of the slope, but cross ways, and at night if we did sleep, we had to lie on the side, all of us on one side, so as to have enough room for all of us. When somebody couldn't bear it any longer, then we would all have to wake up and turn round to the other side. Therefore, the sleeping conditions were terrible. All the clothing we had was what we had on us. They would put a shoe -- people would put a shoe under their heads. We didn't have any blankets at first or anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the toilet facilities and the kind of food you had, food and water, while you were in the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether you can call it food and water, but I'll try to explain. At the bottom of this tunnel, where it was flat, there was a metal can, a container, which was about 15 litres -- it could contain 15 litres, and we had to use it as -- for our toilet needs. After some time precisely above our heads at ground level several prisoners dug out a hole maybe the size of a table which we could use when we were allowed to go out by the guards. In the meantime, when the guards couldn't or were not around to let us out, we had to do what we needed to do inside. The food was mostly three loaves of bread for 45 of us. At least I was the one to carry the bread from the administrative building and later it was Zaro Mrkajic who did it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About how long approximately a period of time was it that you were responsible for bringing the bread from the administration building to the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was for the first fortnight or so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Besides when you were taken out to either use the toilet facilities or when you were allowed out to get the bread, were there other times when you were taken out of the tunnel and, if so, where were you brought?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally was mostly not taken anywhere except to fetch the food. I would regularly be beaten either by some of the soldiers in front of the administration building or the guard himself, depending on who it was, but these were minor slaps or a kick at first or with a fist, but they were not real beatings that affected my health.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, when you were in the tunnel, was the door kept open or closed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The door was mostly closed, if the guards were not in front of the door, or if there was no interrogation going on or any beatings. So the door was mostly closed. Especially at night there were wooden poles that supported the doors and leaning on the steps to keep the doors closed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, other than what's happened -- what happened to you when you were first brought to the camp, that you already described, and the slaps or kicks or being hit with a fist that you also have described, were you ever seriously mistreated while you were at the camp, what you call, I believe, a real beating? (Pause) Is the answer yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please -- I want to try to go chronologically. So if you can please describe the first instance you remember of this treatment, and I ask that you speak slowly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time that I was beaten was, I think, on the third day, because for the first two days we didn't go out, nor did anyone come to see us, as far as I can remember, and when I went to fetch the food I met a young man who knew me very well. I knew him too, but I can't recall his name. We must have met somewhere. The guard was taking me by the scales that were used to weigh freight in the direction of the administration building to get the bread, and he approached me with a smile on his face, as if he was a friend, but when he got to 1 metre from me, he suddenly changed the expression on his face and kicked me in the area of my crotch, and I lost consciousness for a moment. When I came to he was standing above me and he said -- I must apologise to your Honours for the rudeness, if I may be allowed to use the expressions he used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, you may state exactly what was said to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said roughly that I have very hard balls and that we Cetniks are known for this and he kicked me again in the back and then he went off. The guard ordered me to get up but I couldn't get up from the pain. I lay there for about 40 minutes. The guard was kicking me. I can't remember who he was at the time, because I really couldn't believe that all this was happening to me. So I was lost. I was -- I couldn't fully comprehend that this was happening and the guard threatened to kill me if I didn't get up. So I almost crawled to the administration building. I somehow managed to get up, pick up the loaves of bread and return to the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, was that the only time that you were the victim of serious mistreatment, and, if not, could you please tell us the next incident that you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly at first at the very beginning I was not maltreated, but every time we went to use the toilet facilities upstairs, the hole I was talking about, we were lined up against the wall near building Number 9, five to six, to you ten people of us, and we would be hit sometimes once, sometimes twice with a baseball bat or with a rifle butt or kicked in the back, things like that, and this was -- these beatings were almost regular for all of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any time where the beating was more severe than what you've just described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On one occasion I remember that it was still sunny, so we were allowed a little earlier than usual to use the toilet and I was the first in a group of five or six men. I happened to be the first, though I was lying in the middle of the Tunnel Number 9. Hazim was there present when we came out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the full name of Hazim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hazim Delic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue with your account?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I came out, when I was climbing the steps, I saw across the path on the fence there were two of my neighbours sitting there, who used to be my friends. One was called Alija Balic and the other Emin Spiljak. They were sitting there and with them was Hazim Delic. I saw that at that moment Hazim Delic was holding something like a baseball bat in his hand. He ordered us to stand along the wall, to raise up our hands and at that moment I heard one of the two of them say that -- he said: "Hit the first one very hard, because he is my neighbour". I didn't see that, because I was facing the wall. I suddenly felt a terrible pain in my right side. I almost bent over to the right although that is difficult to do, and I was thrown about 1.5-2 metres to the left. I didn't fall. Hazim was behind me and he told me to go and piss. Then I headed towards the hole. Fortunately it was not far away. He hit the other four or five of us that came behind me and all of us came to the hole. When we had finished he ordered us to go back to camp Number 9. From that blow I think up to 1995 I had a swelling here on the right-hand side and later on I was examined by Dr. Mrdzic, but there was no treatment given to me in the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who it was who hit you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was Hazim Delic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were in Tunnel 9 or during the time you were staying in Tunnel 9, were there any other incidents where you were severely mistreated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Beside this systematic beatings I need to say also that there were individual ones. People were taken out, mostly at night. A lot of prisoners. There is Damjan Dordic, Rajko Dordic and most of the prisoners. I cannot say all of them by names, but they were taken out, beaten and brought back in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, with respect at this time to you in particular, was there any other time other than you have described in Tunnel 9 when you were taken out and mistreated or mistreated while you were in the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, personally I was once taken at night by a prison guard, and I will tell a story that came before. That there was during the day and Pavo Mucic was present, we were taken out to go to the toilet up above, and Pavo Mucic was standing at the fence and Zaro Mrkajic was there at all. Pavo Mucic said "who is this last one" and he heard Zaro tell my name. He told my name. However, nothing happened. They took me back and when it became dark the guard called out my name and told me to follow him. This was about 9.00, 9.30. I don't know exactly when it was. It was getting dark in those days. He took me, I think it was the same office where I'd given that statement. A guard was sitting there. We called him Focak. I don't know his exact name. I forgot it. I was sitting there. He was very correct. He even gave me a cigarette. He asked me various questions. He asked me what happened to my personal weapons. I told him I didn't have it. He said where did I give it away. He talked about a brother who was in prison. He was the same age. He was insisting on me giving him some pistol, some pistol which was very old. I told him that I did not have that pistol, that I never had one. He said: "Okay. Go now", but if I did not remember it until the next evening where this pistol was, they would call me again, and that would not be good. Then I said: "You don't need to call me. I really don't know". He said: "No, no, just go and remember" in front of the building there were about seven or eight guards. He told me to follow them to Number 9. However, in this darkness and the light was very dim I was nearly blind at that time. I had not been exposed to enough light in that period. So I was walking along this white line. It is phosphorescent, so there is a little glow. I was following that. They were laughing at that. That way we came to Number 9. Then they told me to stand against a wall and raise my arms. I did so and they started beating me. I started moaning. Then I heard Focak's voice as they were kicking and hitting me with rifle butts. I don't know about other objects. I did not see so well. Then I heard the voice of this Focak saying something like this and I quote: "What are you waiting here for? Let me hit him" then he hit me with something against the back. I felt as if I had been thrown. I fell on the threshold, the threshold to that door and after that I don't recall anything. I woke up and I had a bandage and my head was lacerated at the back. I still have a bump on my head as a result of this. This is one of the instances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you estimate, if you can, approximately when this was that this happened, what month or about how long you had been at the camp approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was some time in late June or early July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You have indicated, sir, that earlier before this beating, earlier that day you had seen Mr. Mucic and he'd asked who you were. Was that the first time you'd seen Mr. Mucic at the camp, or were there times before that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. I think you may have misunderstood me or maybe I misstated it. He didn't ask me. He asked Zaro Mrkajic what my name was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I think maybe there was a translation error. I believe that's exactly what you said and what I understood. Was this the first time that you had seen Mr. Mucic or had you seen him on other occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must say that I did not know Mr. Mucic personally. I did not know how this person looked, but there were other people who knew him, like Zaro Mrkajic and other people, who knew him. I don't know in what way. They knew the car that he was driving and through them I found out that he was the camp commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me go back just for a minute. The person that you came to know as Mr. Pavo Mucic, the day of your beating, was that the first time you had seen Mr. Mucic in the camp or had there been any other occasions prior to that, before that, when you had seen him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had seen him before, that is for sure, but I had not had any direct contact with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you indicate for me approximately how many times you saw Mr. Mucic in the camp during the entire time you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Personally I saw him at least about 20 times, maybe even more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mucic ever come to the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He never walked in, but he came to the door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. What would he do when he came to the door? For what purpose did he come to the tunnel, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the most part he did not contact with myself or with us in general, so he was probably there to see us. I don't know why but he was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever talk -- even if he didn't talk to you, did he ever talk or take out any prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Mostly he and Hazim Delic would talk to Zaro Mrkajic and when there was that last selection, the last transfer of people from 9 to Number 6, Pavo was there. He was present and he asked that everybody come out of this cell so that he could take a look at him. He and Hazim decided who would stay in Number 6 and who would go to Number 9.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately when was this, the incident where Mr. Mucic and Mr. Delic decided who would stay in 6 and who would go to 9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You made a mistake again or it may have been a mistake in interpretation. At least this is how I got it, who was going to stay in Number 9 and who was going to 6, but I think this was after the visit of the ICRC. So that would be some time in August, late August.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, you indicated that Mr. -- you learned that Mr. Mucic was commander of the camp. Can you indicate exactly, if you can, when you learned that and how?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, he made contact with people that he knew, probably -- I don't know for what reasons he chose them. It was through Zaro and we mostly found this through Zaro and through guards who were there. So mostly when he would come to the camp there had to be some kind of a military discipline. At least at that time nobody came in to beat us or to mistreat us. For instance, I heard from Esad Macic, who was a guard in the camp, he would tell us to hurry up, if we had been in the toilet to hurry up and walk in there, because the Commander was coming in this car of his -- I think it was a Toyota. We could see the gate directly and we could see it coming in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately what month or how long you had been in the camp the first time this happened, when you were told that Mr. Mucic was commander of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know but I think it was still in July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, was there ever a time when you were staying in Tunnel 9 that you were taken out of Tunnel 9 and then put somewhere else for some period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On one occasion a group was selected. It was about half of us. I don't know exactly the number, but about half. We stepped outside and we were led in the direction opposite of the gate, so that means away from the gate towards the far end of the camp with our hands behind. One hand had to be behind our back and the other one on the shoulder of the inmate in front of us. There were a lot of guards there. There was Delic and Zenga and all the other guards who were there, and I had the impression that they were taking us -- leading us quite a way, 300 or 400 metres. Given the state we were in, the condition we were in, it was a long distance for us. So we were brought -- I don't know how to call this, but it's a structure. Later I saw that it was a manhole, and this is where we were beaten, and we were pushed in there through some small metal door that was on top of this manhole. This manhole was made -- rises a little bit above the ground. There are several steps and then from there you go down. I don't know exactly what its use was but I know that inside there was a lot of -- some pipes and some fans.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can I ask you, if you could, if you know, could you point out on the model the approximate area or where this was that you were taken, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicating) Here. We were taken out of Number 9 and we went along this road. As I said, it looked a very long distance to me, because I was very exhausted. They brought us to this concrete wall. We climbed up there and this manhole was right there, here somewhere, in this area on the model.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. What happened after you were placed inside the manhole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were pretty much all beaten with some handles. I think they were handles for some agricultural tools. Then the lid was closed and there was some rubber ring around it, so that it was hermetically sealed. There were two pipes. One was -- like air ducts, which were made, I guess, for ventilation. Those two were also closed so there was no air there. We spent about three or four hours there. Then they opened up the manhole and they called out Rajko Vujcic to get the food for us. I think they brought one or two breads and two or three liver pates. As they had taken him by the hands because he had climbed all the way up to that top platform and then they beat him with this handle. We were already without air for a long time. When they had enough of beating him, they threw the bread and the liver pate down. Then the manhole was reopened again only the following day some time in the morning. I don't know how late it was, but I know that night had passed, because I overheard the conversation by the guards, because they said that they had really secured this structure, that we would stand no chance, that they could just withdraw during the night. It was very hot inside. There was no air from any side. I still don't believe to this day that we survived it. That's how long it was that so many people stayed in this space, because the measurements were 2 by 2 and maybe 2.5 to 3 metres high. Anyway, I was already half delirious and I only remember at one point some light appeared from above and I had some air, but I sort of fainted because I think maybe it was because of this rush of fresh air. Then the order came to get out and then the beatings resumed. They lined us up against this concrete wall, which is up from this manhole, and I overheard the guards during the night. They were saying how we were going to be executed with all the usual swear words that accompanied this. Then ten of us were lined up against this wall. At the step of this manhole I saw Hazim Delic and Pavo Mucic standing next to this manhole, and again I was not fully aware, because of this lack of oxygen. With them, next to them, were Rajko Dordic, Desimir Mrkajic and Rajko Mrkajic who was there. I overheard the conversation. It was mostly by Pavo saying that we were to be executed. We were standing against a wall. There were a lot of soldiers there and there were these in placements (sic). Somebody showed up in a car -- I think it was a Golf, a red colour -- and just from the window said it had to be put off. I don't know if he was referring to our execution or what else, but then they -- then they returned us to Number 9 with the usual beating accompanying it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the next incident chronologically where you were mistreated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Number 9 except for the beatings during the time when we would go out to the toilet -- I'm talking about myself, but I have witnessed other beatings. I don't know if that is important to mention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For now I just would like to discuss yours. The incident that you describe where you were put in the manhole, can you give us an approximate date, month or about how long you'd been in the camp when that incident occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think this was already late July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, previously you indicated that when you were hit in the ribs by Mr. Delic with a bat or something that looked like a bat. Can you just describe what this instruments was like and if you had ever seen it -- if you ever saw it on any other occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This was most probably an original baseball bat, a bat used for a game of baseball. It was kind of yellowish. At first I thought it was brass, but later, when I received this blow, I think it was wooden.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the other occasions when you saw this bat, who would have it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Who had it? Mostly Hazim Delic, and when he wasn't around, this Focak had it. It was as necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. During the time that you were in Tunnel 9 did you ever receive any sort of mistreatment, severe or not severe, by this person you referred to as Landzo?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am going to object, your Honour. She is leading the witness. He never said he was mistreated. I am sorry, I got the French interpretation just there. He never said he was beaten by Landzo. She is leading the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I did not suggest he had said it. I just asked. He had mentioned Landzo and I asked if this had ever happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, that is a leading question, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: What, if any, sir, activity did you see this person Landzo engage in while you were in Tunnel 9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he was rarely on a guard post in front of Number 9. For the most part he was not. For the most part he would come either with Hazim or by himself, and one day when Slovko Susic was brought in -- that's how I noticed Landzo the best -- Hazim was beating him and there were some other guards there as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am going to object. I believe he has not said he saw this beating or something like, that the foundation has not been laid on whether he had personal knowledge of what he was talking about at this point. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I think we will have to.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: We will have to stop and continue next time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. You worked very hard for the day. You are getting tired.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That is certainly true, your Honour. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours your Honour, I would like to request that the Prosecutor gives us the names of the next witnesses, because following this witness we only know the name of another witness. This is absolutely insufficient for the preparation of the defence. Also if the Prosecutor could tell us the names of the witnesses -- of those witnesses for whom they think that most probably will not be testifying. Since there was a list of 35 witnesses for which the Defence is preparing, I think that it is necessary for us to get the names of the witnesses who have given up to testify with a possibility obviously that, should these witnesses change their mind again, the Prosecution could give us a list of those witnesses as well. Thank you. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: The Prosecution was complaining of some difficulties in their ability to ascertain who or who is not to get into their witness list. I'm not sure that difficulty is over, but I'm sure they will communicate whoever is their next witness. They are not holding them. It is not for their own personal profit. I am sure they will give you the names. Even if the Trial Chamber says they should give you, it depends on their ability to know who to tell you are the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, just with respect to the court's schedule, if I could have one minute to consult with lead counsel, he has given me a note which, in fact, has to do with the upcoming witnesses. So if you could just give me a few seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: While she is doing that, your Honours, I wonder if -- I had some indication that the question of what days we are sitting next week might still be an open issue. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: I know we are sitting on Monday. At least I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Then so do we. There is a possibility we will be sitting other days next week. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: My timetable doesn't disclose that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have just a kind of a final closing observation. I believe, your Honour, that I have made it through an entire week without insulting anyone. If that's not true, I now apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: My question or answer, or whatever, pertains to this question that your Honour just answered to Mr. Ackerman, whether we sit more than Monday next week. I have an urgent question from the Victims and Witness Unit to go on or not to go on scheduling for other days in next week. Do we have any indication whether there will be more than Monday next week? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: As far as I am concerned, I have not made any other arrangement other than what we decided at the status conference. I know the Tadic Trial Chamber is not sitting next week, but we haven't decided either to sit. So we still retain our earlier decision to sit on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: That's the only day we sit next week? JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you very much, your Honour. JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE: So the Trial Chamber will now rise until Monday morning.
